events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: Well, I do declare — if this isn't the most magnificently spooky entrance hall I have ever had the pleasure of walking into! Look at those portraits, just daring you to blink first. And that chandelier — oh honey, that chandelier is one strong breeze away from redecorating the floor. Now then — a guest book! In an abandoned mansion! If that isn't an invitation to start unraveling a mystery, I don't know what is.
events.thinking: There's a warmth spreading through my chest the moment I step through that door — the kind you get walking into a house that's been waiting for someone. Dust motes drifting in whatever light's getting through, and the air smells like old wood and stories nobody's told in a long time. My fingers are already tingling. Every portrait on that wall has eyes that follow you, and that chandelier looks like it's hanging on by sheer stubbornness. But what I notice first — what my body notices before my head catches up — is the people. Peter's here, and my stomach does that little flip it always does. The boys are here too, bless their hearts, all crowded together like they're already casing the place. And Uncle Sneekly — standing there in that hood like he always does, and I feel that old settling, like coming home. Dick Dastardly's lurking about with Muttley, and I should keep an eye on them, but honestly, right now everyone's here and everyone's whole and the tightness I didn't know I was carrying just... loosened. That guest book, though. A guest book in an abandoned mansion. Now who's been signing that?

events.desc: Every locked door is just a puzzle that hasn't met me yet. And somewhere in this grand old pile of dust and secrets, the Doily Diamond is waiting. I can practically feel it humming through the floorboards.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Ah, welcome, welcome to Doily Manor, one and all! I am Pemberton, the estate manager. I do hope your journeys were not too arduous. If I might direct your attention to the guest book here — a tradition of the house, you understand. Every visitor signs upon arrival. It helps me keep track of... well, of everything.
events.thinking: There's that settling in my chest — the cool stone feeling. I've just arrived. The entrance hall. Dusty, grand, full of people who don't know what I am. Good. My fingers are already mapping the room — Penelope is here, trusting, oblivious. Peter Perfect hovering nearby like a loyal dog. The Ant Hill Mob... there's a prickle at the back of my neck when I notice them watching. They see too much. Dick Dastardly — useful, impulsive, disposable. But my primary concern is Clara. She's not in this room. I need to find her, track her movements, understand where the treasure hunt will lead her. But first — I am Pemberton. The mild-mannered estate manager. I must settle into the role. The guest book on the side table... a natural thing for an estate manager to attend to. It gives me a reason to linger, to observe, to take stock of who is here and who is not. The smile comes easily. It always does.

events.desc: Look at them. Every last one of them trusting, unsuspecting. Penelope practically glows with naivety — she'll sign the guest book without a second thought, and I'll know exactly who is here and who is yet to arrive. Most importantly... where is Clara? She must be somewhere in this wretched manor. The treasure hunt begins soon, and she must not reach the end of it. But patience, Vincent. Patience. The design is everything. First, we observe. Then we arrange.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Right then, lads — we're 'ere. Doily Manor. Blimey, look at the state of this place — chandelier 'anging by a thread, dust thick enough to write your name in. *sniffs* Smells like trouble to me. Now listen — I promised Clara's old man we'd keep 'er safe, and that's exactly what we're gonna do. Nobody lets 'er out of their sight, yeah? *glances at Sneekly* And nobody — *nobody* — gets too cosy wivout us knowin' about it.
events.thinking: There's a tightness behind my ribs the moment I step through the door — not pain, more like a rope going taut. My eyes go straight to her. Penelope. She's here, she's standing, she's breathing. Good. The tightness eases half a notch. But then my neck prickles — that electricity climbing up behind my ears — because *he's* here too. Sneekly. Pemberton. Whatever he's calling himself today. Standing too close. Smiling too easy. My stomach knows before my brain does, same as it always has. The chandelier's hanging crooked overhead and the whole place smells like dust and old money and something I can't name yet. I need to get the lay of this place. Exits. Corners. Blind spots. Where she can run if she needs to.

events.desc: That Pemberton... Sneekly... whatever 'is name is — 'e's already stood closer to Clara than I'd like. Can't put me finger on it exactly, but me neck's pricklin' somethin' fierce. Last time I felt this was when that new kid joined the crew back in Brixton. Three weeks later, the stash was gone. I ain't clever enough to work out what 'e's up to, but me gut don't lie. It never 'as.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Ah, what a MAGNIFICENT establishment! Reginald Foxworth, decorated adventurer and — as it happens — the FOREMOST authority on manor treasures in all of England. You may have heard of my exploits in the Bavarian Crypts? No? The Zanzibar Diamond Affair? Well, no matter — I shan't bore you with tales of my MANY triumphs. Now then, let me just sign the guest book here — purely as a formality, you understand. A man of my stature leaves his mark EVERYWHERE he goes.
events.thinking: There's a fizzing in my fingers already — that tightness behind my eyes that means the room is rearranging itself into levers and sequences. All these fools gathered in one dusty foyer like sheep at a gate. My chest is warm. Not from the welcome — from the count. The guest book, the coat rack, the exits to kitchen and library. Two paths, one treasure, and a room full of useful idiots. The fake medal sits heavy in my pocket like a promise. I can already feel the architecture forming — who to flatter, who to misdirect, who to send down the wrong corridor while I slip away with the prize. Penelope, Peter, the Professor — all earnest, all exploitable. And Sneekly — now there's competition I'll need to watch. But first, intelligence. The guest book. Who's been here, what they've written, what they've accidentally revealed. Every fool signs their name next to their weakness.

events.desc: None of those adventures actually happened, of course. But these gullible fools don't know that. And while they're busy being impressed, I'll be busy reading every name and note in this guest book. Knowledge is power — and power is treasure — and treasure is MINE.

First impressions matter. The guest book — that's the civilised thing. Sign in, establish presence, show that James Hartwell does things correctly. But first... I need to say something. Something that lands. Something with shape to it.

events.desc: Three structural hazards. I've actually only spotted two — the chandelier and that wobbly coat rack — but three sounds more thorough. I'll find the third one. I always do.

events.thinking: The prickling at my scalp has settled into something warmer — everyone's signing the guest book, everyone's talking, the room has that buzzing energy of people arriving somewhere together. Peter called me Miss Pitstop and said nobody's getting hurt on his watch, and there's that familiar flutter in my stomach, the one that's half safety and half something else entirely. The boys are being protective, bless them — Clyde's already got that look, scanning the room like he's working out who to trust. And Pemberton — Uncle Sneekly — he's being so gracious, welcoming everyone. Dick Dastardly's signing with a flourish and talking about himself like he always does, and honestly I find it more entertaining than annoying. But what's pulling at me now is the library. A carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription. An inscription. That's the kind of thing that leads somewhere. Every treasure hunt I've ever been on — and I've been on more than a few, thank you very much — starts with words carved into stone. The guest book was the appetizer. The library is the first course. My feet are already pointed that direction.

events.desc: An inscription on a stone mantelpiece in a mansion hiding a legendary diamond. That's not decoration, sugar — that's the first breadcrumb. Clara Bellingham did not put on her best exploring boots to stand in a foyer all evening.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Ah, splendid, splendid — Mr Foxworth, is it? And Mr Hartwell, how very thorough of you to inspect the premises. I assure you the chandelier has held for forty years, though I confess I do step around it rather briskly myself. Now then — I see we are nearly all accounted for. But I do believe Miss Bellingham has not yet signed in. She may have wandered ahead into the library — the young lady did express an interest in the family histories. If you'll all excuse me, I ought to ensure she hasn't gotten herself turned around. These corridors can be quite... disorienting.
events.thinking: The prickle at the back of my neck — the Ant Hill Mob. 'Nobody gets too cosy wivout us knowin' about it.' That was directed at me. I felt my shoulders tighten before I processed the words. They're watching. They promised Clara's father they'd keep her safe. So Clara IS here — or expected. Good. That confirms she's in the manor somewhere. But the Mob is a complication. They have instincts. Street instincts. The kind you can't charm away with a smile and the right words. Dick Dastardly — 'Reginald Foxworth' — is already signing the guest book, preening, making himself the center of attention. Perfect. Every eye on him is an eye not on me. Peter Perfect — 'James Hartwell' — is already hovering around Penelope, identifying structural hazards. Predictable as clockwork. He'll be wherever she is, which means he won't be wherever I need to be. Now — I need to find Clara. She's not in this room. The library or the kitchen. I should move toward the library — a natural place for an estate manager to direct guests, and if there are clues to the treasure there, I need to see them first. But more importantly, I need to see the layout. Map the exits. Find the places where an accident could happen and no one would question it. The guest book tells me who has arrived. Now I need to know who hasn't — and where the ones who matter are hiding.

events.desc: Clara is somewhere in this manor, and the Ant Hill Mob just told me everything I needed to know — they're her guardians, which means she's valuable, which means she's close. The library. Of course the library. Where the family histories are kept, where the treasure clues begin. I must get there before she finds something I can't undo. And I must get there alone. The smile on my face right now — the helpful, bumbling Pemberton, worried about a lost guest — it fits so perfectly it almost makes me laugh. Almost. But not yet. Gloating is for after.

But Pemberton — 'helps me keep track of everything,' he said. Everything. Not everyone. Everything. My neck does that thing again, that slow electric crawl. The kid with the easy laugh, the one who disappeared with the stash — he was always counting things too. Always knowing where stuff was. I can't say what's wrong because I don't have the words for it. I just know I've felt this prickle before and it's never been wrong. Peter Perfect — Hartwell, whatever — he's fussing about structural hazards, bless him. Means well. Useful muscle if it comes to it. But right now I need to see that guest book. Who's been through here before us? What's Pemberton keeping track of? I'll sign it — got to, haven't I — but I'm reading every name in that book first.

events.desc: 'Keeps track of everything,' he says. Not 'keeps a record of guests.' Not 'tradition of the house.' Everything. Now maybe that's just how posh people talk — I wouldn't know, would I? But on the streets, when someone wants to know where everything is, it's because they're planning to move it. Or move you. I'm gonna read every bleedin' name in that book.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Well, well, WELL! Most illuminating, this guest book. Most illuminating INDEED. You know, in my extensive experience — the Bavarian Crypts, the Zanzibar affair, the incident in Monte Carlo which I am LEGALLY forbidden from discussing — the first clue is ALWAYS found near the hearth. The KITCHEN hearth, specifically. Old manor houses like this one always hid their valuables near the cooking fires — something about the heat protecting the parchment. It's a well-known fact among us professional treasure hunters. I suggest you ALL make haste to the kitchen immediately. Every moment you waste here is a moment the clues grow COLDER — quite literally! I shall join you presently — I simply must finish making some scholarly notes first.
events.thinking: The guest book — I've signed it, I've read it. Peter Perfect is also poking at it, the earnest fool. And he pulled Penelope aside for a private chat — probably pledging to protect her or some such nauseating chivalry. My fingers are tingling. The cool tightness is settling behind my eyes. Two exits: kitchen and library. The library has a carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription — that's where clues live. That's where treasure maps hide. The kitchen is copper pots and a stove — nothing of value to a man of my ambitions. But here's the architecture forming: if I announce loudly that the KITCHEN is where the treasure clues are, these fools will stampede toward the pots and pans while I slip quietly into the library to read that inscription. The hollow behind my navel is pulling — I need to move, to claim, to get there first. And that estate manager Sneekly — something about him makes the hair on my neck prickle. He's too smooth. Too welcoming. But no — I'll give him the benefit of the doubt. People deserve trust until they prove otherwise. Focus on the plan. Misdirect the herd, slip into the library alone.

events.desc: There is absolutely no scholarly basis for treasures being hidden near kitchen hearths. I made that up entirely. But the beautiful thing about a confident lie is that nobody checks. While these credulous simpletons rummage through copper pots and flour bins, yours truly will be in the library, reading that inscription on the stone mantelpiece. The LIBRARY, you see — THAT is where a proper manor keeps its secrets. Inscriptions, hidden compartments, false bookshelves — the architecture of deception! And I should know. I AM the architecture of deception.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: There we are — James Hartwell, signed and dated, proper ink. I always say, a man who doesn't sign the guest book is a man with something to hide. Now then! I couldn't help but notice that chandelier — it's listing a good fifteen degrees to starboard, which means the mounting bracket has sheared at least two of its four anchor points. I've seen this before in Victorian load-bearing ceilings — the plaster key degrades and the whole fixture becomes a pendulum waiting for an excuse. I propose — and I've thought about this carefully — that nobody stands directly beneath it until I've had a chance to inspect the ceiling joists from above. Miss Pitstop, might I suggest you stand just here, by the staircase? Structurally the soundest position in the room. I checked.
events.thinking: The guest book is under my hands now — leather, cracked, cold to the touch. My fingers find the pages and there's a small satisfaction in the gesture, the formality of it. Everyone's arriving, making their entrances. Dastardly — or whatever he's calling himself, Foxworth — is already posturing, and I can feel that familiar tightness in my jaw when someone performs confidence without earning it. But it's Sneekly who keeps pulling at the edge of my attention. 'Helps me keep track of everything,' he said. Everything. The way he said it — too smooth, too rehearsed. My neck prickles again. But no — Father taught me better than that. You don't accuse a man on a feeling. You watch. You prepare. And the Ant Hill Mob — good lads, they're watching Clara too. That eases something in my chest, knowing I'm not the only one standing between her and... whatever this place has in store. Now — I've signed the book, I've made my entrance. The library. Books mean maps, records, histories of the house. If there's a treasure here, the clues will be in the architecture of the place — structural, methodical. And if I can find something before anyone else, something I can bring to Clara's attention with proper gallantry... that hot weight behind my sternum pulses. Yes. The library first. But I should look at this room more carefully — that chandelier, the portraits. A thorough man examines what's in front of him before charging ahead.

events.desc: I haven't actually checked the ceiling joists. Or the staircase's structural integrity, for that matter. But the staircase is solid oak — you can tell by the grain — and it puts her three good paces from the chandelier's fall radius. That much I did calculate. The rest... well. James Hartwell will figure out the rest. He always does.

Penelope Pitstop: Oh, would you look at this! 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' Now that, ladies and gentlemen, is not just decoration — that is the first real clue in this entire mansion! And the answer, if I am not very much mistaken, is a map. A map! Which means somewhere in this library — tucked between these dusty old books, or hidden behind this very mantelpiece — there is a map waiting for us. And I would bet my grandmother's music-box key that it leads straight to the Doily Diamond!
events.thinking: Oh, my heart is hammering. The library — the smell of it hits me first, old leather and dust and something underneath, like the air itself has been holding its breath for years. The mantelpiece is right there, carved stone, and I can already see the letters from across the room. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' The answer lands in my chest before my mind catches up — it's a map. A map! The prickling at my scalp is electric now, the same feeling from grandmother's attic, from the cave. Something is here. Something is waiting to be found. But I also notice — Uncle Sneekly followed me in, and Dick Dastardly too, and those two big fellows, Rock and Gravel. Peter stayed behind. The boys stayed behind. There's a tiny pull in my stomach, the awareness of who's not in the room, but it's thin — the curiosity is louder right now, much louder. The inscription is a riddle, and the answer is a map. And if there's a riddle on a mantelpiece, there's something behind that mantelpiece, or inside it, or triggered by it. My fingers are already warm. I need to interact with it.

events.desc: A riddle on a mantelpiece. A map as the answer. And a diamond at the end of the trail. Clara Bellingham, you did not wear your exploring boots for nothing. Now — let's see what happens when you give this mantelpiece the answer it's been waiting for.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Ah, the library! One of the manor's finest rooms, if I do say so. The late Lord Doily was quite the bibliophile — spent years assembling this collection. Now, I see Miss Bellingham hasn't made it here after all. How curious. I do hope she hasn't found her way down to the cellars — dreadfully unsafe, those cellars. Now then, I couldn't help but notice the inscription on the mantelpiece there. Lord Doily was fond of his puzzles, rest his soul. I believe the treasure hunt begins with that very riddle. 'Cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish.' I confess I am only a humble estate manager — puzzles were never my strong suit. But I'm sure one of you brilliant guests will crack it in no time!

Now, I have been in a great many libraries in my time, and I can tell you that books do not turn themselves upside down. Someone put them that way deliberately. And in my experience — which involves a grandmother's attic, a locked box, and a very determined five-year-old — when something is out of place on purpose, it's pointing you toward the next step. Let's see what these contrary little books have to say for themselves!

Clara's here, Pemberton's here, Dastardly's at the mantelpiece lookin' far too interested in that inscription for a man who claims to be an adventurer, and now these two. Between 'er and anyfing that moves wrong.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Yes, yes, Miss Pitstop — a MAP, very good, how ASTUTE of you. I was JUST about to say that myself, naturally — the globe is merely the INTERMEDIARY step, which any EXPERIENCED treasure hunter would know. First the globe, THEN the map, you see. But never mind all that — what NONE of you have noticed is that this mantelpiece has a SECONDARY mechanism. You see this groove here? This circular indentation? In the Bavarian Crypts — which I PERSONALLY explored — these mechanisms require a medallion. A SPECIFIC medallion. And as it HAPPENS — purely by coincidence, you understand — I carry with me at ALL times a medal of distinguished service, awarded to me by the Royal Geographic Society for my contributions to — well, the point IS, stand back everyone, stand BACK! Let the professional handle this!

The architecture isn't ruined — it's just... revised. I need to use this medal on the mantelpiece before anyone else figures out there's a mechanism. Peter's here now too. The Ant Hill Mob. The room is getting crowded. Time is compressing. I can feel it thinning — the window closing. But the medal is mine. The mechanism is mine. Act now. Talk later.

A FAKE medal might be the REAL key! If this works — if this mantelpiece opens and reveals the treasure — then Reginald Foxworth will have done what none of these honest, earnest, PLODDING fools could manage. Won with a lie. Won with a counterfeit. Won with ARCHITECTURE. My hands are trembling. This is it. THIS is the moment!

Something that represents those things without containing them. A map. It's a map. The answer is a map. Three sleepless nights building a bridge — this is nothing. I know this answer. The weight behind my sternum shifts from hot urgency to something warmer. This is what I can build. This is the thing no one can look away from.

Some kind of medallion or disc. And I do not have one — yet. So the question becomes: where in this magnificent old house would Lord Doily have hidden the key to his own puzzle? Now, Clyde, sweetheart — I am just fine, you don't need to stand guard over me like I'm made of porcelain. But I am delighted you're here. events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: 'Ere — 'ERE! Everybody slow down a minute! *steps back from the mantelpiece, nearly backing into one of the reading chairs, which scrapes loudly across the stone floor* We've got Foxworth stickin' medals into walls, Pemberton rootin' around in the bookshelves talkin' about 'idden compartments — *wheels around to face the Hooded Claw* — 'idden compartments, 'e says! Like 'e knows exactly where to look! Funny, that, for an estate manager. Most estate managers I've met know where the boiler is, not where the secret panels are! *realises he's said too much, catches himself* I mean — not that I'm sayin' anyfing by that. I'm sure it's all very... above board. Very professional. It's just — *moves to position himself between Penelope and the bookshelves where Sneekly is working* — it's just that maybe we should all be a bit more careful about pullin' fings and pushin' fings and stickin' medals into fings before we know what they DO, yeah? For safety! Like Hartwell said — safety first! Right, Hartwell?
events.thinking: Everything's moving fast and my body can't decide what to do with it. There's a warmth in my chest because Clara's right here, safe, talking about her grandmother and upside-down books — she's brilliant, she is, even when she's walking straight into danger without knowing it. But then the prickling comes back hard because Pemberton — Sneekly — he's at the bookshelves now, talking about hidden compartments, saying 'allow me' like he owns the place. Allow him what? To find whatever's hidden before anyone else does? And Dastardly just shoved a fake medal into the mantelpiece like some kind of nutter. A fake medal. From the Royal Geographic Society. Pull the other one, mate. Something about that groove in the mantelpiece though — a circular indentation. That's a lock. That's a proper mechanism. And Dastardly just stuck his dodgy medal in it. What if he triggered something? What if something's about to — my shoulders are squaring again. Too many people doing too many things at once and Clara's standing right in the middle of all of it. I need to watch Pemberton at those bookshelves. He said 'hidden compartments' and 'things disappearing into the walls.' He knows this place. He knows it too well.

events.desc: Listen to me — 'most estate managers I've met.' I ain't met a single estate manager in me life. But I know when someone knows too much about a place they're supposed to just be managin'. Pemberton went straight for those books. Straight for 'em. Didn't browse, didn't wonder, didn't hesitate. That's a man who's been through them shelves before. And Dastardly wiv his medal — that's either the most ridiculous bluff I've ever seen, or 'e came 'ere wiv that thing on purpose. Either way, Clara's standin' between a man who knows where the walls open and a man who brought 'is own key. And 'ere's me, Danny from Brixton, who can barely read the inscription on the bleedin' mantelpiece. But I can read people. And right now, every person in this room is readin' like a bad cheque.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: AH HA! Just as I SUSPECTED! The medallion has ACTIVATED the first stage of the mechanism — you see, these Victorian puzzle-locks operate in SEQUENCES, not single steps. The medallion was merely the PRIMER. Now the REAL work begins! And if you'll all notice — as I noticed IMMEDIATELY, being a trained professional — several of those books on the shelves are placed UPSIDE DOWN. That is NOT a coincidence. That is the SECOND stage! The medallion primes the lock, the books complete the sequence — it's EXACTLY like the Venetian Cipher Vault of 1847, which I personally — well, never mind THAT story, we haven't got TIME! Pemberton, step ASIDE from those shelves — you'll trigger the mechanism in the wrong ORDER and we'll ALL be locked in here for a CENTURY!
events.thinking: I 'fussed with the mantelpiece for a moment.' That's it. That's ALL it says. No dramatic reveal, no hidden compartment springing open, no treasure tumbling into my waiting hands. I fussed. Like a man adjusting his cufflinks at a funeral. The fake medal didn't work. Or it did something I can't see yet. My inventory is empty now — the medal is gone, consumed by the mechanism, and I have NOTHING to show for it. The hollow behind my navel is yawning wide open. I had ONE unique asset and I spent it on a mantelpiece that gave me nothing back. Meanwhile — MEANWHILE — Sneekly is already at the bookshelves, turning the upside-down books. Penelope noticed them too. The upside-down books. That's the next clue, isn't it? The books that are deliberately wrong. And I'm standing here with empty hands and an empty inventory, having just made a spectacle of myself with a tin medal from Croydon. My jaw is tight. My stomach is that cold hollow — plate after plate disappearing before mine arrived. But no. NO. Reginald Foxworth does not STAY defeated. The bookshelves. The upside-down volumes. Sneekly is already there but the Ant Hill Mob and Peter are still fussing with the mantelpiece. I need to get to those bookshelves. And I need a new angle — a new scheme. The medal is gone but my MIND is not. Those bookshelves are the next step. Move. NOW.

events.desc: The medallion did absolutely nothing. Nothing at all. It sat in that groove like a penny in a wishing well — useless, inert, and now lost forever. Six pence, gone. But do these fools know that? They do NOT. As far as THEY know, I've just activated a hidden Victorian puzzle-lock sequence that only a trained professional would recognise. And now I need to get to those bookshelves before Sneekly does — because SOMETHING is hidden there, and whatever it is, it's MINE. The scheme adapts. The scheme ALWAYS adapts. That's what separates Reginald Foxworth from the common criminal — ARCHITECTURE.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: My jaw tightens. Dastardly — Foxworth — just claimed credit for the map answer, twisted it into his own narrative, and now he's fumbling with the mantelpiece with some bogus medal. The hollowness behind my ribs flickers — that old feeling of standing next to someone louder, watching them take up all the space. But then it passes, because she noticed. Penelope noticed the upside-down books. She's sharper than all of us. And Sneekly — he's already at the bookshelves, reaching for them, saying it's his 'responsibility.' The prickle at my neck sharpens. He's trying to get to whatever's hidden before anyone else. But I can't prove bad intent. Father would say watch, don't accuse. The upside-down books — that's the real clue. Not the mantelpiece mechanism, not Dastardly's fake medal. The books. Several volumes placed deliberately upside down. That's a code, a sequence, a message. My hands are already itching. This is the kind of problem I was built for — methodical, structural, something you solve by being thorough. Sneekly is already interacting with them, though. I need to get to those bookshelves. But I should do it properly — offer to help, position myself between Sneekly and whatever he's reaching for, and examine the books systematically. That's both gallantry and protection in one gesture.

Penelope Pitstop: Now, everyone — I can see we are all getting rather excited, and I love that energy, I truly do. Peter and Clyde, you two keep working on those upside-down books — Peter's system is exactly right, top to bottom, left to right. Mr. Foxworth, do try not to jam anything else into that beautiful mantelpiece until we know what goes there, there's a dear. But here is what I am thinking: Uncle Pemberton just went into the laboratory, and he mentioned Lord Doily kept all manner of instruments and devices in there. A laboratory full of brass instruments, in a house with a puzzle that needs a medallion? Now, I am not a gambling woman, but if I were, I would bet my grandmother's music-box key that whatever fits that circular indentation is sitting in that laboratory right now. So I am going to follow Mr. Pemberton and have myself a look. Every locked door is just a puzzle that hasn't met me yet!
events.thinking: There's a buzzing under my skin now, that electric restlessness that won't let me stand still. Sneekly just left — slipped into the laboratory talking about lubricant for the shelving mechanism. That's interesting. He knows this house better than anyone, and he went straight for the laboratory. And Clyde — bless him — he's getting suspicious of Sneekly, positioning himself between me and the bookshelves, talking about how Pemberton knows exactly where the hidden compartments are. My stomach does a little twist at that, not because I think Clyde's wrong to be cautious, but because I can feel the air in the room changing. Voices are getting sharper. Dick is shouting about Venetian cipher vaults. Clyde is practically accusing Sneekly of something. Peter is being methodical but I can feel him tensing up too. The harmony is fraying at the edges and my body knows it before my mind — that old dinner-table tightness creeping in. But the curiosity is stronger right now. Sneekly went to the laboratory. The laboratory has brass instruments and a machine with gnawed wires. If there's a medallion or a tool that makes the bookshelves work, it's probably in there. Peter's working the bookshelves with the boys — they've got that handled. I should follow Sneekly. Not because I don't trust him — I do, completely — but because the laboratory is the next room in the chain and my feet are already pointed at that door. The cave girl in me doesn't wait at the entrance.

events.desc: Clyde's suspicions about Pemberton are sweet but misplaced — Uncle Sneekly has been managing this estate for decades, of course he knows where the compartments are. That's his job, sugar. But the laboratory... the laboratory is calling to me the way that cave did when I was eleven. Something is in there. Something round, something brass, something that fits a hole in a mantelpiece. And Clara Bellingham is going to find it.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with rufus-ruffcut.
events.thinking: My breathing slows the moment I step through the doorway. The laboratory. Brass instruments catching what little light filters through grimy windows. Bubbling flasks — still active after all this time? Someone has been here recently. The machine dominates the far wall — levers, dials, a gauge, and that gnawed wire hanging loose like a severed tendon. 'Requires 3 operators.' Three. That's important. It means the machine can't be activated alone, which means it can't be used as a simple trap — not without accomplices. But a gnawed wire... if the wire were reconnected incorrectly, the machine could malfunction. Overheat. Spark. And if someone happened to be standing near those bubbling flasks when it did... The workbench — tools but no wrench. Interesting. The wrench is missing, which means someone took it, or it's hidden deliberately. The crates in the corner — could contain anything. And the cellar connects from here. A damp stone cellar. Another exit, another route. My fingers are mapping the room already, the way they used to map the estate ledgers. Two new faces — Rufus Ruffcut and Sawtooth. Large, rough-looking. The kind of men who work with their hands. Potential operators for a three-person machine? Useful. Very useful. But first — I need to understand what this machine does. And those crates. The Ant Hill Mob's words are still buzzing in my ears — 'hidden compartments, he says, like he knows exactly where to look.' He's suspicious. He's watching. I need to be more careful, more Pemberton, less Vincent. For now.

events.desc: The machine requires three operators. Three. And a wire has been gnawed through — which means it's broken, which means it's DANGEROUS, which means it is absolutely, exquisitely perfect. Picture it: Clara wanders into the laboratory, curious, trusting, the way she wanders through everything. I convince two others to help 'test' the machine — perhaps the Slag brothers, or these two rough fellows here — and when the gnawed wire sparks at just the wrong moment... But no. Too direct. Too traceable. The estate manager who suggested testing a broken machine? Even Hartwell would see through that. I need something more elegant. Something where I'm not in the room when it happens. Something where the machine activates while Clara is alone, or where she activates it herself, thinking it's part of the treasure hunt. Yes. YES. Weave the machine into the puzzle trail. Make the treasure hunt itself the weapon. The clue in the library leads here, and the machine becomes the next 'challenge' — and the broken wire becomes the blade hidden inside the game. My jaw is unclenching. I can feel that deep, settling stillness. The design is almost whole.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: My gut just clenched. Pemberton's gone. He slipped out to the laboratory while everyone was arguing about books and medals. 'Just popping through to fetch some lubricant,' he said. Lubricant. For stuck shelves. In a laboratory full of brass instruments and bubbling flasks and — what did it say — a machine with many levers and dials. He's alone in there now. Alone with whatever Lord Doily kept in his workshop. And Clara called me 'sweetheart' and told me not to stand guard like she's made of porcelain. That stung. Not because she's wrong — she's not porcelain, she's the toughest person I know — but because she doesn't see what I see. She doesn't feel the prickling. She trusts people because she's good, and good people think everyone else is good too. That's why she needs me. Not because she's weak. Because she's blind to the bad ones. And right now one of the bad ones has just walked into a room full of machines. Alone. I should follow him. But if I leave Clara here with Dastardly and the Slag brothers... No. Hartwell's here. Peter's solid. He'll watch her. I need to see what Pemberton's doing in that laboratory.

events.desc: Clara told me not to stand guard. Called me 'sweetheart' like I'm one of 'er bleedin' lapdogs. And it hurt, yeah — because I ain't doin' this for thanks. I'm doin' this because 'er old man looked me in the eye and said 'Watch over 'er, Danny.' And a promise to a dead man don't come wiv conditions. She can call me whatever she likes. I'll still be standin' between 'er and whatever's comin'. But right now, what's comin' might be in that laboratory. Pemberton didn't go for lubricant. Nobody goes to a laboratory for lubricant when there's a perfectly good kitchen down the 'all. 'E went because 'e wanted to be alone wiv whatever's in there. And Danny from Brixton is about to find out what that is.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Ah yes, the bookshelves — FASCINATING, truly fascinating. I can confirm that the upside-down volumes are EXACTLY as I predicted — part of the sequential mechanism. Now, I must confess, my EXTENSIVE training in Victorian puzzle architecture tells me that the THIRD stage requires — ah — a specific solvent. An oil, if you will. And I couldn't help but notice that our good Mr Pemberton mentioned lubricant in the LABORATORY. As the ONLY qualified professional here, I really ought to supervise him — can't have an estate manager tampering with delicate mechanisms unsupervised, can we? You all continue with the books — EXCELLENT work, truly — Peter, your systematic approach is almost as thorough as mine would be. I shall return MOMENTARILY with the necessary supplies!
events.thinking: Sneekly has slipped away to the laboratory. He said he was fetching lubricant but that's obviously a lie — he's going after something in there. The machine with the gnawed wire. Something important enough that he manufactured an excuse to leave the room while everyone else was distracted by the bookshelves. I interacted with the bookshelves but the summary doesn't tell me I found anything dramatic. Peter and the Mob are also poking at them. Penelope is surveying the room. Everyone is HERE, clustered around these shelves, doing the honest work of examining books — and Sneekly, the one person who actually KNOWS this house, has just walked out. My gut is telling me two things at once. The hollow is pulling — follow Sneekly, because wherever he's going is where the real prize is. The cool tightness behind my eyes is sequencing — let these fools do the bookshelf work, let them find whatever the upside-down books reveal, and meanwhile I follow the man who actually knows where the treasure is hidden. Sneekly is the thread. He's been steering everyone — 'oh I'm just a humble estate manager' — but the Ant Hill Mob noticed it too. He knows where the secret panels are. He knows this house. And now he's alone in the laboratory. This is the bread roll moment. Everyone's looking at the bookshelves. Nobody's watching the door. I slip out. I follow. I take what he finds before he can pocket it. The architecture is simple this time — and simple is better. My elaborate schemes keep backfiring. This time: follow the man who knows, take what he finds.

events.desc: Sneekly knows something. He LEFT. While everyone was distracted by books and riddles, the one man who knows every secret passage in this house slipped away to the laboratory — alone. That's not fetching lubricant. That's a man going to collect something he's been keeping for himself. And Reginald Foxworth — who has just lost his only possession to a groove in a mantelpiece, who is standing here with EMPTY HANDS and EMPTY POCKETS like the youngest boy at the table again — is NOT going to let another helping disappear before it reaches him. I'm following that snake. And whatever he finds in there, it's MINE.
events.thinking: Sneekly has slipped away to the laboratory. He said he was fetching lubricant but that's obviously a lie — he's going after something in there. The machine with the gnawed wire. Something important enough that he manufactured an excuse to leave the room while everyone else was distracted by the bookshelves. I interacted with the bookshelves but the summary doesn't tell me I found anything dramatic. Peter and the Mob are also poking at them. Penelope is surveying the room. Everyone is HERE, clustered around these shelves, doing the honest work of examining books — and Sneekly, the one person who actually KNOWS this house, has just walked out. My gut is telling me two things at once. The hollow is pulling — follow Sneekly, because wherever he's going is where the real prize is. The cool tightness behind my eyes is sequencing — let these fools do the bookshelf work, let them find whatever the upside-down books reveal, and meanwhile I follow the man who actually knows where the treasure is hidden. Sneekly is the thread. He's been steering everyone — 'oh I'm just a humble estate manager' — but the Ant Hill Mob noticed it too. He knows where the secret panels are. He knows this house. And now he's alone in the laboratory. This is the bread roll moment. Everyone's looking at the bookshelves. Nobody's watching the door. I slip out. I follow. I take what he finds before he can pocket it. The architecture is simple this time — and simple is better. My elaborate schemes keep backfiring. This time: follow the man who knows, take what he finds.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Right — Clyde, you're absolutely right. Safety first. Nobody touches anything they don't understand, and that includes Mr Foxworth's enthusiastic medal-jabbing. Now — I've examined the bookshelves, and here's what James Hartwell can report. Miss Pitstop identified the upside-down volumes, and she was right — they're deliberate. But the shelves themselves have a mechanism, and it's stuck. Pemberton said he was going to the laboratory for lubricant, which — well, I'm sure he knows best about the house's maintenance needs. But I notice he left rather quickly, and I notice the laboratory is through that door right there, and I notice we now have one fewer pair of eyes on proceedings. I'm not suggesting anything untoward — I believe in giving people the benefit of the doubt. I'm merely... noting it. For the record. Now — Miss Pitstop, you mentioned a circular indentation, a slot for a medallion. That's our missing piece. A map needs a key, a lock needs a key, and somewhere in this manor is the key to this particular puzzle. I propose we search this room thoroughly before anyone goes wandering off into laboratories alone. Who knows what's behind these books once we get the mechanism unstuck?
events.thinking: The prickle is gone from my neck — Sneekly left. He slipped away to the laboratory while everyone was talking. 'Lubricant,' he said. For stuck shelves. My gut doesn't believe him. My gut thinks he's gone to do something he doesn't want witnesses for. But Father's voice is there too — you don't chase a man down on a feeling. You watch, you prepare, you give him the rope to prove himself one way or the other. What I can do right now is stay here, stay close to her, and work the puzzle. The bookshelves — I interacted with them. The upside-down volumes. Penelope said we need a medallion for the mantelpiece, a disc of some kind for that circular indentation. And Dastardly is claiming his fake medal did something, which it obviously didn't. The Ant Hill Mob — Clyde — he's sharp. He caught the same thing I caught about Sneekly. 'Hidden compartments, he says, like he knows exactly where to look.' Good man. But he's also watching me, measuring whether I'm an ally or competition. I need to show him I'm on his side. On her side. Same side. The warmth across my shoulders settles — this is the gathering weight, not the bright surge. I'm in assessment mode. What do these upside-down books tell us? Where is the medallion? And where did Sneekly really go?

Good. If Sneekly is up to something, at least two of us are watching. And if he isn't — well, James Hartwell will be the first to apologise. With grace. With proper form. Because that's what good men do.

events.thinking: The smell hits me first — chemicals and metal and something faintly burnt, like a match struck hours ago. My hands are warm and tingling, fingers already reaching for surfaces before my eyes have finished cataloguing the room. Brass instruments, bubbling flasks — bubbling! Something is still active in here, which means this laboratory isn't as abandoned as everything else. The machine is enormous, all levers and dials, and there's a gnawed wire hanging loose — mice, Sneekly said. 'Requires 3 operators.' That's interesting. Lord Doily never had three people he trusted. That's sad and useful information at the same time. The workbench has tools but no wrench — someone took the wrench, or it's been deliberately removed. And those wooden crates in the corner... crates are where you put things you want to store, or things you want to hide. My scalp is prickling the way it did in grandmother's attic when I found the locked box behind the summer curtains. The crates feel right. But I also notice — Clyde followed me in. He tripped over a chair on the way, bless him, and he's positioning himself again, watching Sneekly. And Dick came too, probably hoping to get to whatever's in here first. The room feels crowded with intentions. Sneekly is examining the machine. The crates are calling to me. Old wooden crates in a Victorian laboratory — that's where you hide something you want found eventually but not immediately. Let me look at them.

events.desc: Crates in the corner of a mad inventor's laboratory. The workbench has been picked clean of its wrench — someone's been here before us, or the wrench is part of another puzzle elsewhere. But those crates... they're sitting there like grandmother's locked box, just waiting for the right curious girl to come along and start trying keys.

events.thinking: A jolt of cold alertness — everyone followed me. Penelope, the Ant Hill Mob, Dastardly. They're ALL here now. The laboratory that was supposed to be my private reconnaissance has become a crowded stage. My shoulders tighten. The Mob — I can feel their eyes on me like a hand on the back of my neck. They followed me specifically. 'Where'd Pemberton go?!' — I can practically hear the suspicion in that voice. This is a problem. I'm being watched too closely. I need to deflect, to redirect. The machine — I've examined it. Three operators, gnawed wire. But I can't do anything with it while they're all staring at me. I need to pivot. The crates — what's in the crates? And the cellar connects from here. A damp cellar with 'surprisingly cheerful decorations' and air vents. Someone has been REDECORATING the cellar? That's... unexpected. That's not Pemberton's doing. Someone else has been in this manor, preparing something. That prickles. That prickles a lot. But right now, with the Mob watching my every move, I need to be aggressively Pemberton. Helpful, bumbling, slightly overwhelmed by all these guests. I should draw attention to the machine as a puzzle element — make it seem like part of the treasure hunt, plant the seed that it needs to be activated. Then step back. Let curiosity do my work for me. And I should interact with the crates. An estate manager checking inventory — perfectly natural. But really I'm looking for something I can use. A tool, a clue, anything that gives me an edge.

events.desc: Oh, this is DELICIOUS. I just told them the machine is connected to the treasure. I told them it's dangerous. And I told them not to touch it. Which means — given Penelope's insatiable curiosity and Dastardly's greed — someone will absolutely touch it. I've planted three seeds in one speech: the machine matters, it's dangerous, and it requires three people. Now all I need is for Clara — Penelope — whoever she IS in this scenario — to be one of those three operators when that gnawed wire decides to spark. The Mob is watching me, yes. But what they just heard was a concerned estate manager warning everyone about a safety hazard. How very RESPONSIBLE of Pemberton. How very, very responsible. Meanwhile — those crates. If there's a wrench in there, or tools, I can pocket them. Control the means of repair. If the machine can only be fixed with a wrench that only I possess... well. Then I decide when it works, and when it doesn't. And THAT is architecture.

events.thinking: The prickling is everywhere now — climbing my neck, settling behind my ears, spreading across my shoulders. This room smells like metal and something chemical I can't name. Clara followed Pemberton in here. She followed him. I told Hartwell to keep her in the library and she walked right past him because that's what Clara does — she walks toward danger like it's a puzzle to solve, not a thing that can hurt her. And now she's in a room with bubbling flasks and a machine with gnawed wires and Pemberton is asking about wrenches and talking about Lord Doily's secrets. 'Never had three people he trusted enough.' That's a strange thing for an estate manager to know. That's intimate knowledge. That's not managing an estate — that's knowing a man's fears. And Dastardly followed too. Everyone's in here now except Hartwell and the others in the library. The crates in the corner — what's in them? The machine — gnawed wire, needs three operators. Something about this room feels like a trap that hasn't sprung yet. My hands are closing into fists and I don't remember telling them to.

events.desc: She's 'ere. In a room full of fings that could hurt 'er. And I can't drag 'er out because she's Clara Bellingham and she don't get dragged anywhere. So I do what I always do — I stand between 'er and the worst of it and I pretend I ain't terrified. Pemberton knew Lord Doily didn't trust people. He knew it personal-like. That ain't somefing you learn from a job interview. And those crates I just backed into — they shifted too easy. Like they've been moved recently. Like someone's been in 'ere before us, movin' fings around. I want to look in them crates. But first I need to make sure Clara don't touch that machine wiv the chewed wire.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Ah, Pemberton! There you are! I was DEEPLY concerned — a man of your advanced years, wandering unaccompanied through a laboratory full of volatile chemicals and unstable machinery! It's a good thing I came to supervise. Now then — this machine is CLEARLY a Lord Doily original — I've seen its EXACT design before in the Austrian Imperial Workshops. 'Requires three operators,' yes, yes — a standard Victorian triple-action compression engine. Terribly dangerous if improperly calibrated. I would STRONGLY recommend that EVERYONE focus their attention on this machine — it's CLEARLY the centrepiece of the treasure hunt. In fact, I insist — Miss Pitstop, Mr Ruffcut, Clyde — all of you, gather round the machine. Study it CAREFULLY. Every dial, every lever. I shall inspect the rest of the room for, ah, SAFETY hazards. Fire exits and such. One can never be too careful in a Victorian laboratory!
events.thinking: My hands are empty. That's the sensation — open palms, nothing in them, the specific lightness of having spent your last coin on a bet that didn't pay. The medal is gone and I'm standing in a laboratory with Sneekly, Penelope, the Ant Hill Mob, and two people I don't know — Rufus Ruffcut and something called Sawtooth. The room is crowded AGAIN. My plan to follow Sneekly alone has been foiled by the same problem as the library — everyone had the same idea. Penelope followed him. The Mob followed him. I followed him. We're all here, watching each other watch Sneekly. But — the crates. Wooden crates in the corner. Nobody's mentioned them yet. And the machine — requires three operators, gnawed wire. Sneekly said Lord Doily never had three people he trusted. That's interesting. That's a lever. But the crates — the CRATES are what my hands want. Something is in those crates. Something nobody else is looking at because they're all fascinated by the big shiny machine with its levers and dials. The bread roll was in the pocket, not on the table. The treasure is in the thing nobody's watching. The crates. While everyone gawks at the machine and interrogates Sneekly, I check the crates.

events.desc: While every set of eyes in this room locks onto that magnificent machine with its three-operator sign and its gnawed wire — a puzzle DESIGNED to attract attention, DESIGNED to make people cluster and cooperate — Reginald Foxworth will be over in the corner, quietly opening those wooden crates that NOBODY is looking at. The crates, you see. Always the crates. The treasure is never in the thing everyone's staring at. It's in the thing nobody noticed. I learned this at age six, at a dinner table where the good pieces went to the first three and the youngest got the scraps — unless the youngest learned to look where nobody else was looking.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: She — Miss Pitstop went into the laboratory. After Pemberton. After I specifically suggested we search this room first. Right. Right! James Hartwell does not stand in an empty library talking to bookshelves while the woman he — while a lady walks into an unfamiliar laboratory with a man whose knowledge of hidden compartments is suspiciously detailed! Gentlemen — Rock, Gravel — I am going to ask you a tremendous favour. These bookshelves have a mechanism connected to those upside-down volumes. The mechanism is stuck but the clue is in the sequence. If either of you could keep an eye on things here — don't pull anything, don't push anything, just... guard the shelves — James Hartwell would be in your debt. I need to go and make sure Miss Pitstop doesn't — that is, I need to inspect the laboratory for structural hazards. Which I'm sure it has. Laboratories always have structural hazards. Coming through!
events.thinking: Cold. The room is suddenly cold and too quiet. She left. She went into the laboratory — after Sneekly — and I'm standing here looking at bookshelves. The steel plate behind my ribs slams into place so hard it takes my breath. This is the country road. This is the engine ticking. This is the dark and the headlights not yet visible and her walking toward them while I stand here cataloguing dust. Clyde told me to stay here with her and she left anyway. She went toward the man who makes my neck prickle and I recommended we search the library thoroughly and she — she just went. And now it's me and the Slag brothers in an empty room full of upside-down books. My hands are shaking. Not from fear — from the wrongness of being here when she's there. Every second I spend looking at these shelves is a second she's in a room with someone I don't trust and I'm not between them. But — but. The books. The upside-down volumes. If I leave now, I lose whatever the bookshelves are trying to tell us. If I stay, I lose her. No. Not lose her. She's not mine to lose. She's in the next room, not the next county. Clyde is with her. Dastardly went too. She's not alone. She's capable. She chose to go. But that doesn't help the feeling. Nothing helps the feeling except being there.

events.desc: She chose to go. She is perfectly capable of looking after herself. She has Clyde and his mob and even Dastardly between her and trouble. James Hartwell knows all of this. James Hartwell is going anyway. Because the bravest and stupidest thing he's ever seen is himself, running after a woman who didn't ask to be followed, because standing still when she's out of sight feels like the country road and the dark and the engine ticking and no way to shield anyone from whatever comes next.

Dick is trying to herd everyone toward the machine, which is suspicious — why does he want us all gathered around one thing while he inspects the rest of the room? That's the oldest trick in the book, and I may trust everyone by default but I'm not blind, sugar. He wants the crates to himself. If we could fix that gnawed wire...

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Heat floods my neck. She called me 'Uncle Pemberton.' UNCLE. That word lands like a slap — not because it's wrong, but because it's exactly right. That's what I am to her. Uncle. The trusted family fixture. The man who manages everything while she inherits everything. The word crystallises something in my chest — that old, familiar calcification. She trusts me so completely she's given me a family title I never earned and never wanted. And yet — it's useful. It's so terribly, beautifully useful. 'Uncle Pemberton, what does this machine do?' 'Uncle Pemberton, is this safe?' She'll walk into any room I point her toward. Meanwhile the Mob is practically vibrating with suspicion. 'There ain't a drop of lubricant in sight!' He's right, of course. There isn't. My excuse is tissue-thin and he can see through it. But what can he DO? He has no proof. He has instinct, and instinct doesn't hold up when 'Uncle Pemberton' is standing right there being helpful and concerned. Now — the crates. I interacted with them. What did I find? Dastardly and the Mob were also poking at them. The room is impossibly crowded. Everyone followed me. I can't scheme in a fishbowl. I need to separate from the group. The cellar — 'surprisingly cheerful decorations, someone has been redecorating.' That's suspicious and worth investigating. But more than that, it's a room that connects from here. If I can lure Clara — Penelope — through the laboratory into the cellar, that's two rooms away from the entrance hall. Two rooms away from help. Air vents in the walls... My skin prickles. The design is taking shape but I can't refine it with six pairs of eyes on me.

events.desc: Uncle Pemberton. She called me UNCLE. The warmth in that word — it should mean something, shouldn't it? To a normal person it would. To me it means access. It means she'll follow where I lead without question. And I've just done something rather elegant, if I do say so myself. I've suggested Hartwell — the protector, the engineer, the man who inspects everything — should go check the cellar FIRST. Which means he leaves this room. Which means Penelope is here without her most capable guardian. The Mob will follow Hartwell or stay with Penelope, but they can't do both. I'm splitting the defence. And if the cellar really has been redecorated — with air vents — then someone has already prepared it for something. I don't know what. But I intend to find out. Because if there's a room in this manor that's already been prepared as a trap... well. Why build one when someone has done the work for you? All I need to do is change the target.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Something warm cuts through the prickling. Clara called me 'darling.' Asked me to help with the crates. Not 'stand back,' not 'stop fussing' — 'would you be a dear and help me.' That lands somewhere deep, in the place where the bread crust memory lives. She sees me. She sees me as useful, not as a nuisance. The warmth spreads behind my ribs and for a second the prickling thins. But then Dastardly's voice cuts through — 'everyone gather round the machine, I'll inspect the rest of the room.' The rest of the room. The crates. He wants everyone looking at the machine while he goes through the crates. That's a distraction. That's a con. I've run that exact play on the streets — get everyone looking one direction while you clean out the other. And Pemberton's pointing at the crates too, saying Lord Doily hid things in them. Two men, both wanting to get into those crates, both trying to steer Clara toward the machine. My hands close. I need to get to those crates first. Clara asked me to help and that's exactly what I'm going to do — but I'm opening them before either of those two gets a chance to palm whatever's inside.

events.desc: Dastardly wants everyone round the machine while 'e searches the room. Pemberton's pointing at the crates like 'e already knows what's in 'em. Two blokes, same target, different angles. On the street we call that a pincer — one distracts, the other lifts. Well, Danny from Brixton might not know what a 'triple-action compression engine' is, but 'e knows a lift when 'e sees one settin' up. I'm openin' these crates meself. Whatever's in 'em, it goes to Clara first. Not Dastardly. Not Pemberton. Clara.

events.desc: Everyone is whispering. Everyone is clustering. Penelope has her little alliance with the Ant Hill Mob. Sneekly is slithering between conversations like oil through gears. Peter Perfect has arrived to conduct yet another SAFETY INSPECTION. And Reginald Foxworth is standing here with EMPTY HANDS having found NOTHING in those crates worth announcing. But I noticed something none of them did. The CELLAR. Sneekly told everyone the cellars were 'dreadfully unsafe' — but the description says someone has been REDECORATING down there. Cheerful decorations in a cellar that the estate manager warned us away from? That's not a cellar. That's a LAIR. Someone — Sneekly, almost certainly — has been using that cellar for something he doesn't want guests to see. And while these fools huddle around machines and crates like moths at a lamp, the REAL treasure is one floor below their feet. Silent departure. No announcement. No theatrical exit. For once in my life — and it PAINS me to do this quietly — I am going to slip away without a single soul noticing.
events.thinking: I interacted with the crates. But the Ant Hill Mob ALSO examined them — at the same time. So much for my quiet, unseen approach. And Sneekly was whispering to Penelope. The Mob was whispering to Penelope. Everyone is whispering. Everyone is scheming. And I'm the one who's supposed to be the schemer! My jaw aches from clenching. The result just says I interacted — no detail about what I found. But here's what I notice: there's a cellar exit from this room. A damp stone cellar with cobwebs, old furniture, and — 'surprisingly cheerful decorations, someone has been redecorating.' Someone has been REDECORATING the cellar. Sneekly earlier warned people away from the cellars — said they were 'dreadfully unsafe.' But someone has been decorating down there. That's wrong. That's the hinge nobody's watching. The estate manager tells everyone the cellar is dangerous, but someone's been making it cheerful? That's Sneekly hiding something. That's where the real action is. Everyone in this room is clustering around crates and machines and whispering to each other. The cellar is one room away, nobody's mentioned going there, and Sneekly actively discouraged it. The bread roll. The thing nobody's watching. My gut pulls downward — time is thinning. But the cool tightness is also there, behind my eyes, and it's saying: go where nobody else is going. The cellar. Now. While they're all busy with their whispered alliances and their crate-poking.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: The warmth hits my shoulders the instant I see her. She's here. Safe. Examining the crates with that look she gets — the one where her whole face sharpens and you can see the puzzle-solving happening behind her eyes. The steel plate loosens. I can breathe again. But now I'm taking in the room properly and my hands are already twitching. A gnawed wire on a machine that requires three operators. A workbench with no wrench. Bubbling flasks — active chemicals in an unsupervised laboratory. Every single thing in this room is a hazard or a mystery or both. And Sneekly is here, hovering near the crates, talking about Lord Doily's hiding spots like he's reading from a script he wrote himself. My neck prickles again. But I notice something else too — this machine. Brass and copper, levers and dials, requires three operators. That's not a decoration. That's functional. And the gnawed wire means it's broken — or sabotaged. Someone — or something — disabled it. If this machine is connected to the treasure, and if the riddle in the library leads here, then fixing this machine might be the next step. And fixing things... fixing things is what James Hartwell does. The hot weight behind my sternum shifts from anxiety back to that old familiar hunger. Build something. Fix something. Show her you're the one who can.

events.desc: I said 'reliable person' while very carefully not looking at Sneekly. Clyde would be the obvious third. Or Rufus — he looks like a man who knows his way around machinery. But not Sneekly. Not Dastardly. Not until I understand what this machine does and who benefits from it being broken. James Hartwell is already planning three steps ahead. This is what he does. This is the bridge competition all over again — except the bridge is a Victorian machine and the judges' table is wherever Penelope is standing.

events.thinking: The machine is beautiful and broken. Brass and copper, levers and dials, a gauge — and that gnawed wire hanging like a severed thread. My fingers itch looking at it. Three operators. Peter and I are two — we need one more. But the wire needs fixing first, and the wrench is missing from the workbench. So: find wrench, fix wire, gather three people, operate machine. That's the chain. But something else is pulling at me — Sneekly just mentioned the cellar. Cobwebs, old furniture, and 'surprisingly cheerful decorations — someone has been redecorating.' Who redecorates a cellar? That detail is like an upside-down book — it doesn't fit, and things that don't fit are where I need to look. And Dick just slipped away into the cellar while everyone was talking. He's down there right now, alone, probably searching for something. The cellar also has air vents along the upper walls, which is an odd detail to mention. And Sneekly suggested Peter go down to check structural soundness — was that helpful, or was that getting Peter away from me? No. No, Uncle Sneekly wouldn't do that. He's just being thoughtful. But my stomach did a tiny flip when he suggested it, and I'm not sure why. The social harmony pull is strong right now — Clyde scattered tools everywhere, he's wound up, the tension between him and Sneekly is like static electricity. But the curiosity pull is winning. The cellar is the next unexplored room. Dick went alone. And someone has been redecorating down there. That's not right. That's the seam, the gap, the thing that doesn't fit. I need to go look.

events.desc: Someone has been redecorating the cellar. Redecorating. In an abandoned mansion where everything else is dust and cobwebs. That is the detail that doesn't fit, and Clara Bellingham does not leave details that don't fit uninvestigated. Dick Dastardly is already down there, and whatever he's up to, I intend to find out — not because I suspect him of anything terrible, but because a treasure hunt is a team sport whether he likes it or not.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Oh dear — did Mr Foxworth just wander off into the cellar? By himself? I did specifically warn about those steps! The stonework down there hasn't been maintained in years — one wrong step and... well, I shouldn't like to think about it. I'd better go after him before he hurts himself. Miss Bellingham, Mr Hartwell — please do wait here. I'll have him back in a moment. As estate manager, I really can't have guests injuring themselves on the property. The liability alone would be quite... quite dreadful.
events.thinking: A tightness across my shoulders — Dastardly has gone to the cellar. ALONE. Without permission, without announcement, he just... slipped away. That prickle at the back of my neck sharpens into something harder. He's in MY cellar. The cellar I was going to use. The cellar with the cheerful decorations and the air vents that someone prepared for SOMETHING. And now Dastardly — greedy, impulsive, uncontrollable Dastardly — is down there, probably rifling through everything, probably contaminating whatever setup exists. My jaw tightens. A variable slipping loose. Someone acting outside the pattern I set for them. The restless insomnia feeling floods back — that tightness behind the sternum, the fingers working. I need to get down there. But Penelope just defended me to the Mob — 'Uncle Pemberton has managed this estate for decades, and if he knows where the hidden compartments are, well, that's because it's his job to know.' She DEFENDED me. That warm expansion in my chest — the settled rightness. She moved exactly as my words arranged. The Mob's suspicion deflected by Penelope's trust. Architecture. Beautiful architecture. And Hartwell wants to operate the machine with Penelope — 'Miss Pitstop, if you and I and one other reliable person were to operate it together once I've repaired that wire.' He's planning exactly what I planted. The machine, three operators, the wire. But he wants to REPAIR it first. Predictable, thorough Hartwell. If I can find the wrench before he does, I control whether it gets repaired — and HOW it gets repaired. The workbench has tools but no wrench. The wrench is the key. Where is it? The cellar? The kitchen? The entrance hall? Dastardly is in the cellar NOW. I should follow him — ostensibly to fetch him back for safety, but really to see what's down there before anyone else does. And to find that wrench.

events.desc: Dastardly has gone to the cellar alone, and I cannot allow that. Not because I care about his safety — I couldn't care less if he fell down every step — but because that cellar has been PREPARED. Someone redecorated it. Someone installed air vents. And I need to know why before anyone else does, because whatever purpose that room was designed for, I intend to redesign it for MINE. And here's the beautiful part — by chasing after Dastardly to 'save' him, I look like the responsible estate manager once again. The Mob can't follow me AND stay with Penelope. Hartwell won't leave her side. So for the first time since I arrived at this wretched manor, I will have a room to myself — or near enough. Just me and Dastardly, and Dastardly is a tool, not an obstacle. The wrench isn't on the workbench. It isn't in the crates. Which means it's somewhere I haven't looked yet. The cellar is my best chance. And if I happen to discover something down there that advances my design... well. The design is everything. And I am so very close to finishing it.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Clara told me to calm down about Pemberton. Said he's managed the estate for decades, that knowing the hidden compartments is his job. And maybe she's right. Maybe I am being — what did she say? Watching him like he's about to steal the silver. Maybe that IS what I'm doing. And maybe I'm wrong. The boss proved 'family' with medicine when my mum was sick, and I nearly didn't trust that either because I'd seen too many promises break. Maybe Pemberton is just... a bloke doing his job. Maybe I'm seeing ghosts because I grew up seeing them. But then — but then Dastardly just slipped out to the cellar while everyone was busy. Just like Pemberton slipped out to the laboratory. One after another, peeling off from the group, heading deeper into the house. My neck's still prickling. Clara's words settle something in my chest but they don't reach the back of my neck. The neck knows what it knows. And right now it knows Dastardly is alone in the cellar and there's a reason for that. The crates had old equipment and machine oil — Pemberton was right about that at least. Nothing hidden, nothing dangerous. Maybe I AM wrong about him. But I'm not wrong about Dastardly. That man brought his own medal to a strange house. Nobody does that unless they've done their homework.

events.desc: Clara softened me and she was right to — I was wound too tight about Pemberton. The crates proved 'im right about the oil. Maybe 'e IS just an estate manager who knows his house. But Dastardly? Dastardly brought a medal to fit a lock 'e shouldn't have known about. Dastardly tried to send everyone to the kitchen while 'e stayed behind. Dastardly wanted everyone round the machine while 'e checked the room. And now Dastardly's gone to the cellar alone. That's three times 'e's tried to separate from the group, three times 'e's tried to get ahead of everyone else. On the streets, we 'ad a word for people like that. We called 'em the advance man. The one who goes in first and takes what 'e wants before the others even know there's somefing to take.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Well, well, WELL — what have we HERE? A cellar that the estate manager SPECIFICALLY warned everyone away from, and yet someone has been down here REDECORATING! How very curious. How TERRIBLY curious. Cheerful little touches, furniture moved about with care — this isn't a forgotten cellar at all, is it? This is someone's little SECRET. And Reginald Foxworth has FOUND it while everyone else is upstairs playing with machines and books like CHILDREN at a fairground!
events.thinking: The damp hits my skin first — cool, clammy, like the cellar knows I don't belong here. But under that, warmth. Real warmth. Because I'm ALONE. Well — not alone. Three characters I don't know. Big Gruesome, Little Gruesome, Red Max. But nobody from upstairs. No Penelope solving riddles before I can. No Peter Perfect conducting safety inspections. No Ant Hill Mob bumping into things and watching Sneekly. I'm in the place Sneekly told everyone to avoid. 'Dreadfully unsafe, those cellars.' And yet someone has been REDECORATING. Cheerful decorations. Furniture rearranged with care. This is where someone has been spending time. This is someone's secret space. The furniture — 'rearranged with surprising care' — and the air vents, 'just big enough for something very small to explore.' My hands are tingling again. The cool tightness behind my eyes is back, and the room is already sorting itself into levers and sequences. The furniture has been moved. Why? To hide something underneath? To create a specific arrangement? And those air vents — they connect somewhere. Maybe to the laboratory above. Maybe to other rooms. This is the hidden architecture of the house. The thing below the thing everyone else is looking at. My palms are warm. The hollow in my gut is quieter — because for the first time since I arrived, I might actually be ahead of everyone else. The furniture. Start with the furniture. It's been arranged deliberately — and whatever it's hiding is mine.

events.desc: I'm ahead. For the first time since I walked into this wretched manor, I am genuinely, truly AHEAD. Everyone else is clustered in the laboratory, whispering and poking at crates and staring at that three-operator machine. And I — I am in the cellar that Sneekly didn't want anyone to find. The furniture has been rearranged with CARE. That means someone has been down here recently, moving things around — hiding things, or revealing things, or building something. And those air vents — 'just big enough for something very small' — that's a passage. A route. A way to move things through the house unseen. This is the REAL architecture of Doily Manor. Not the riddles and the bookshelves and the machines — those are the PERFORMANCE. This is the MECHANISM. And for once — for ONCE — the youngest boy at the table got to the bread roll first.

events.thinking: My hands are already reaching for the machine before my brain catches up. The gnawed wire — I can see exactly where the break is, exactly how the copper strands have frayed apart. My fingers know what to do. This is the bridge competition. This is three sleepless nights. This is the thing I was built for. But I don't have a wrench, and I don't have wire to splice with. The workbench has tools but no wrench — Sneekly is examining the workbench right now, and I notice he's doing it with a very specific kind of attention. Not searching. Cataloguing. Like he already knows what's there and what isn't. My neck prickles. Dastardly's gone to the cellar — slipped away while everyone was focused on the machine and the crates. Two people have now left the group. Sneekly toward the tools, Dastardly toward the cellar. And the crates — Clyde is searching them. Penelope examined the machine too. She noticed the same things I did. Of course she did. She's always been sharper. But I'm the one who can fix it. That's my lane. That's where the hot weight settles — not in the clever observation, but in the hands that can make it work. I need wire. Copper wire. Or something to splice with. The workbench might have what I need even without the wrench. And those crates — Clyde's searching them. Maybe the wrench is in there. Maybe the wire is in there. I should check the workbench properly myself.

events.desc: I said 'I can absolutely fix this' with the same quiet certainty I felt watching my bridge take the weight. The difference is that bridge had been tested three times before the competition. This machine I've known for approximately ninety seconds. But the principle holds — if it was built by human hands, it can be fixed by human hands. And if those hands happen to be mine, and if she happens to be watching... well. That's the whole point, isn't it? That's always been the whole point.
