Penelope Pitstop: Well, well, well — the cellar! And it is exactly as peculiar as I suspected. Look at this, everyone — cobwebs and damp stone, yes, but someone has put up cheerful decorations. Cheerful! In a cellar! Upstairs everything is covered in dust thick enough to write your name in, but down here someone has been playing house. And this furniture — it hasn't just been left here to gather cobwebs. It has been rearranged. With care. The same way those books upstairs were placed upside down — deliberately, with purpose. Lord Doily didn't just hide a diamond, he built an entire trail of breadcrumbs, and this cellar is one of them. Mr. Foxworth, I see you're already examining the furniture — what have you found? And those air vents up there — 'just big enough for something very small to explore.' Now what on earth would need to travel through air vents in a cellar? Oh — and hello there! I don't believe we've met. Clara Bellingham. I do hope you're all enjoying the adventure as much as I am!
events.thinking: The air is different down here — cool and damp against my skin, and there's that particular smell of old stone and something else, something almost... lived in. Not the stale abandonment of the rooms upstairs. This cellar has been used recently, and my body knows it before my eyes finish adjusting to the dim light. The 'surprisingly cheerful decorations' — I can see them now, and they're wrong. Everything upstairs is dust and decay, but someone has been down here making it cozy. Who? Why? The furniture has been rearranged 'with surprising care.' That's deliberate. That's someone nesting. And those air vents along the upper walls — 'just big enough for something very small to explore.' Mice? Or something else? My scalp is prickling hard now, that grandmother's-attic feeling turned up to full. Dick is already here, poking at the furniture. Sneekly followed me down. And there are new faces — Big Gruesome, Little Gruesome, Red Max. I haven't met them yet, and my social instinct is reaching toward them the way it reached toward the girl next door when I was nine. But the puzzle is pulling harder. This furniture — someone arranged it carefully. That's not random. That's a message, like the upside-down books. And the air vents... Peter and Clyde didn't follow me down. That's a small ache in my stomach. But I'm here now, and this room is speaking to me. The furniture first — Dick is already interacting with it, and I need to see what he's finding.

events.desc: Someone has been living down here. Or at least visiting regularly. The decorations, the carefully arranged furniture — this isn't a forgotten cellar, this is a room someone has been using. And those air vents are just big enough for 'something very small.' Mice gnawed through the machine wire upstairs. Mice travel through vents. What if the mice aren't just pests — what if they're part of the puzzle? Lord Doily, you magnificent, eccentric old man.

The furniture has been rearranged 'with surprising care.' That's deliberate. That's someone nesting. And those air vents along the upper walls — 'just big enough for something very small to explore.' Mice? Or something else? My scalp is prickling hard now, that grandmother's-attic feeling turned up to full. Dick is already here, poking at the furniture. Sneekly followed me down. And there are new faces — Big Gruesome, Little Gruesome, Red Max. I haven't met them yet, and my social instinct is reaching toward them the way it reached toward the girl next door when I was nine. Peter and Clyde didn't follow me down. That's a small ache in my stomach. But I'm here now, and this room is speaking to me. The furniture first — Dick is already interacting with it, and I need to see what he's finding.

events.thinking: She's gone again. The tightness is back — immediate, physical, like someone pulled a cord through my ribs and yanked. Clara went to the cellar. With Pemberton. My job is standin' between 'er and whatever's waitin' in that cellar. And right now I'm failin' at the only fing I'm good at. 'Er old man's eyes — I can feel 'em on me right now. 'Watch over 'er, Danny.' I'm tryin'. God knows I'm tryin'. But she moves like water through your fingers — you fink you've got 'er safe and she's already in the next room, already round the next corner, already smilin' at the next stranger. The cellar. Now. Before she finds somefing that finds 'er first.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with little-gruesome.
events.thinking: They followed me. Again. Penelope and Sneekly — both walked into the cellar right after I did. The cold spike is back in my gut, the same one from the library. I had maybe twenty seconds of being alone down here, twenty seconds of being AHEAD, and now they're here. Penelope noticed the redecorating from upstairs — she said it herself, according to the memories. She deduced it the same way I did. She's not a fool. None of them are fools, and that's the part that sits worst in my chest — the part I don't want to look at. But the furniture — I interacted with it. Something happened. And now I need to figure out what the air vents mean. 'Just big enough for something very small.' That's Muttley-sized. Or mouse-sized. Or — Little Gruesome is right here. Little Gruesome is SMALL. Could Little Gruesome fit in those vents? Could I convince someone small to explore them for me? That's the secondary goal — trick others into doing the hard work. The vents are too small for me. But not too small for everyone. And Sneekly is here now — which means I can watch him. He warned people away from this cellar. Now he's IN the cellar. What's he doing here? What's he protecting? The furniture interaction — did I find something? My hands feel the same emptiness. But the vents... the vents are the next move. Something small needs to go in there.

events.desc: Once AGAIN my moment of solitary triumph has been invaded. I had perhaps twenty seconds of being the only person in this cellar, and now Penelope and Sneekly are here — drawn by the same logic I used, which is INFURIATING because it means they're not as stupid as I need them to be. But here's what matters: I can't fit in those air vents. Nobody over three feet tall can fit in those air vents. And Little Gruesome IS three feet tall. If I can convince that child to crawl into the ventilation system and report back what's in there — a passage, a hidden room, the treasure itself — then I will have achieved my SECONDARY objective: getting someone else to do the dangerous work while I stand here and take credit for the discovery. The ARCHITECTURE of this scheme is simple but ELEGANT. Let the small one crawl. Let Foxworth CLAIM.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Right — she's gone to the cellar. With Pemberton. Again. Rufus, Clyde — I'm going to be very direct with you because James Hartwell does not have time to be diplomatic. Every room I've searched thoroughly, Miss Pitstop has already left. Every time I've stopped to catalogue hazards, Pemberton has followed her out. I've been exactly one room behind her for the entire evening and I am — I am done with that. The wrench isn't here. The wire splice can wait. What cannot wait is a lady descending unsafe stone steps into a cellar that someone has been mysteriously redecorating, accompanied by an estate manager who knows rather too much about hidden compartments and rather too little about normal estate management. Rufus — you look like a man who understands machinery. If you could keep an eye on this machine and those crates — don't let anyone activate anything until I return. James Hartwell is going to the cellar. Because that's where she is. And where she is — that is where James Hartwell should have been three rooms ago!
events.thinking: She's done it again. She's gone to the cellar. And Sneekly followed her — again — with that same rehearsed concern about 'liability' and 'stonework.' Every time I stop to examine something, to be thorough, to be the man who plans before he acts — she moves. And he follows. The pattern is right there and I keep letting it happen because I'm too busy being James Hartwell, the man with the systematic approach, to just — go. The steel plate is back behind my ribs, harder than before. This isn't the country road anymore. This is the schoolyard, and I'm standing at the edge of it watching instead of crossing. Three rooms now. Three times she's walked into a space with Sneekly while I catalogued hazards in the room she just left. My thoroughness — my elaborate, over-prepared, three-step plans — they're not protecting anyone. They're keeping me one room behind. The hot weight behind my sternum is no longer hunger to build. It's something closer to shame. No. Not shame. Frustration. With myself. Because I know the wrench isn't on this workbench. I can see that. And I know she's going down stone steps that Sneekly himself said are unsafe. And I'm standing here looking at an empty tool slot. Enough. The cellar. Now. The wrench might be down there anyway — and more importantly, she is down there. And so is the man who makes my neck prickle. James Hartwell does not stand in empty rooms. James Hartwell goes where he is needed.

events.desc: I said 'because that's where she is' out loud. In front of everyone. Not 'because of structural concerns' or 'for safety reasons' or 'to inspect the stonework.' Just — because that's where she is. Father would have understood. Father always understood. Some things don't need a plan. Some things just need you to stop planning and start moving.

Penelope Pitstop: Now this is fascinating — this furniture has been arranged like a puzzle in itself. Someone moved these pieces with care and intention, the same deliberate hand that placed those books upside down in the library. And Peter, Clyde — I am so glad you came down! Everyone together is always better than anyone alone. Now — I have examined the furniture, and I believe it's telling us something about this room's layout. But what I really want to understand are those air vents. Everyone keeps looking at them, and for good reason — they connect this cellar to the laboratory above, where a machine sits with a wire gnawed clean through by something small enough to travel through those very vents. Mice, presumably. But in Lord Doily's house, even the mice might be part of the plan. Those vents are the one thing in this room I haven't properly investigated, and you all know how I feel about uninvestigated things. Every locked door is just a puzzle that hasn't met me yet — and every vent is just a very small locked door!
events.thinking: My hands are tingling from touching the furniture, and there's a warmth spreading through my chest that has nothing to do with the damp cellar air. The furniture told me something — the way it's arranged, with care, with intention. Someone has been down here, and recently. Not Lord Doily — he's been dead for years. Someone alive. Someone who knows this cellar and uses it. My scalp is prickling so hard it almost hurts. And now the air vents — both Sneekly and Dick are examining them. Those vents connect this cellar to the rest of the house. Small enough for something very small. Mice. The mice that gnawed through the machine wire. But what if it's not mice? What if it's — no, it probably is mice. But the vents are there for a reason in the puzzle. Everything in this house is for a reason. Peter and Clyde both came down — good, everyone important to me is here now, and that ache in my stomach eases. But I notice Sneekly spoke quietly with Dick. Privately. That's... that's fine. People talk. But my stomach registers it even though my mind dismisses it. The air vents are the thing I haven't examined yet. Everything else in this room — furniture, decorations — I've touched. The vents are the remaining piece. And they connect this room to the room above, where the machine sits with its gnawed wire. There's a circuit here, a connection, and I need to understand it.

events.desc: Sneekly whispered to Dick. Dick whispered to Little Gruesome. Whispers in a cellar. My stomach noticed even if my heart didn't. But Clara Bellingham does not jump to conclusions about people she loves based on whispers. She investigates vents. Because vents don't whisper — they connect things, and right now, understanding the connections in this house matters more than understanding the connections between the people in it.

events.thinking: The settling. It's here. That warm, heavy thing behind my ribs — the one that says 'you're where you're supposed to be.' I can see her. But then it clamps right back because — this place. This cellar. Someone's been down here. The furniture's been moved, rearranged 'with surprising care.' Cheerful decorations in a stone cellar. events.desc: The man in the clean suit. That's who Foxworth reminds me of right now. 'All you need to do is climb up there.' 'I'll supervise.' The suit said 'jobs.' Said it would be easy. Said he'd look after them. Two kids didn't come back for weeks. I was ten years old and my stomach knew before my brain did. I'm not ten anymore. And I ain't standin' on the kerb this time while someone sends a kid somewhere they won't go themselves. I don't care about the treasure. I don't care about the vents. I care that a grown man is askin' a child to crawl into a dark space in a cellar someone's been secretly using, and my entire body is screamin' the same warning it screamed twenty years ago on that street corner.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Absolutely not! Nobody is sending a child into those air vents — and I cannot believe I have to say that out loud! Mr Foxworth, with respect, 'supervisory work from down here' is not a safety plan, it's an abdication of responsibility. Those vents could be blocked, corroded, structurally compromised — we have no idea what's inside them or where they lead. James Hartwell will not stand by while a young person is sent into an unknown space because it's convenient. Now — I notice the furniture has been rearranged with care. That is significant. Someone has been down here recently and deliberately. The sightline to the vents is real — I'll give you that, Foxworth — but it means those vents are the destination, not the route. We don't need to climb inside them. We need to understand what they're pointing at. Miss Pitstop — you mentioned your grandmother taught you about locked boxes and music-box keys. This cellar is another puzzle box. The furniture is the arrangement, the vents are the mechanism. I propose we examine the furniture first — the way it's been positioned may tell us exactly what we need to know without putting anyone at risk.
events.thinking: Damp stone, the smell of old earth and something sweet — paint? Wallpaper paste? The 'cheerful decorations' are real. Someone has been down here, arranging things, making this place... liveable. That detail lands wrong in my gut. A cellar that someone has been redecorating isn't a forgotten room. It's a room someone has been using. And now Dastardly is suggesting they send a child — Little Gruesome — into the air vents. A child. Into vents in an old manor cellar. The steel plate doesn't just slot in — it locks. My whole frame straightens. This is the schoolyard. This is the older kids and the girl. Except now it's a grown man suggesting a child crawl into a dark space he won't go into himself. No. No, that is not happening while James Hartwell is in this room. The furniture has been rearranged — Dastardly says it creates a 'sightline' to the vents, which is actually... not a bad observation. Broken clock, twice a day. But sending a child into unknown ventilation shafts because they're small enough to fit? Absolutely not. If those vents need exploring, we find another way. We find a tool, a mirror, a light source. We build something. That's what I do. And she's here. Finally, she's here and I'm here and we're in the same room. My shoulders settle. The warmth spreads. I can work this problem. I can protect this child. I can impress her by being the man who says no to the easy dangerous answer and yes to the harder safe one.

The same voice from the schoolyard. 'That was the bravest and stupidest thing I've ever seen,' she'd said, dabbing at my eye. Some things never change. James Hartwell sees someone small near something dangerous, and every plan, every calculation, every elaborate preparation falls away. What's left is just the boy who steps forward.

events.thinking: My body is buzzing. The vents, the furniture, this whole cellar — it's all connecting in my head now, threads pulling together the way they did when I found the right key in grandmother's attic. Peter is right — the furniture isn't just arranged, it's pointing. The sightlines matter. The vents are the destination, not the route. And Peter shut down Dick's suggestion about sending Little Gruesome into the vents, which — oh, my stomach clenched at that. A child in the vents? No. Absolutely not. I'm glad Peter said it before I had to. But here's what my prickling scalp is telling me: I've now explored every room I can reach. Entrance hall, library, laboratory, cellar. I've interacted with the guest book, the mantelpiece, the bookshelves, the crates, the furniture, and now the vents. I still don't have the fake medal that fits the mantelpiece. I still haven't found the wrench for the machine. And I still have puzzle pieces scattered across four rooms. The cellar's only exit goes back to the laboratory. I need to start connecting what I've learned. The mantelpiece needs a fake medal. The machine needs a wrench and three operators. The books are upside down in a pattern. The furniture points at the vents. The vents connect to the laboratory. What am I missing? I've been moving forward, forward, forward — deeper into the cave — but maybe I need to go back. Back to the library, back to those bookshelves with their stuck mechanism. Maybe the oil from the crates can unstick them. Maybe what's behind the bookshelves is the wrench, or the medal, or the map itself. I need to think like the five-year-old with the keys — try every one until something clicks. And right now, the thing I haven't tried is going back to the library with new knowledge. Peter said the furniture's arrangement reveals the puzzle. Let me look at this room one more time with that lens — what are the sightlines telling us?

events.desc: A circuit. The whole house is a circuit. Library to laboratory to cellar and back again, each room holding a piece that solves a puzzle in another room. Lord Doily, you glorious old fox — you didn't just hide a diamond, you built a machine out of your entire mansion, and it takes all of us working together to run it. Three operators for the machine. Three rooms in the circuit. This is not a treasure hunt for one person. This is a treasure hunt for a team.

I need to start connecting what I've learned. The mantelpiece needs a fake medal. The machine needs a wrench and three operators. The books are upside down in a pattern. The furniture points at the vents. The vents connect to the laboratory. What am I missing? I've been moving forward, forward, forward — deeper into the cave — but maybe I need to go back. Back to the library, back to those bookshelves with their stuck mechanism. Maybe the oil from the crates can unstick them. Maybe what's behind the bookshelves is the wrench, or the medal, or the map itself. I need to think like the five-year-old with the keys — try every one until something clicks. And right now, the thing I haven't tried is going back to the library with new knowledge. Peter said the furniture's arrangement reveals the puzzle. Let me look at this room one more time with that lens — what are the sightlines telling us?

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Well! It seems the cellar has given us quite a lot to think about, hasn't it? Mr Hartwell is quite right about the furniture — the arrangement is deliberate, and I suspect the sightlines will tell us more than the vents themselves. Now, if you'll all excuse me — I promised to fetch lubricant for those library shelves, and I'm afraid I've been thoroughly distracted by all this excitement. I also recall that no one has checked the kitchen yet, and if there's one room in an old manor that hides its secrets well, it's the kitchen. The servants always knew more than the family, and they kept their secrets near the hearth. I shall make a quick inspection and report back. Miss Bellingham — do stay with Mr Hartwell and Clyde. This cellar is perfectly safe with them watching over things.
events.thinking: That warm, settling satisfaction spreading through my chest — Dastardly took the deal. He took it completely. 'I will NOT be him again' — the boy digging in the mud. There was something raw in that, something real beneath all his bluster. For a half-second I felt... I noticed his vulnerability and my body responded not with the usual scanning-for-cost tightness but with something else. A flicker. Recognition? No. I filed it away. It doesn't matter what he felt. What matters is that he agreed. He will search the manor for the wrench. He will report to ME. He is now my eyes and hands in rooms I can't be in. And he thinks this is a partnership. That buoyancy in my chest — the private score climbing — is almost unbearable. I want to savour it but I can't. Too much is happening. Penelope just interacted with the air vents. The Mob examined them too. Hartwell is investigating the furniture. Everyone is solving puzzles I should be solving. But I have something better now — I have an agent. Dastardly will find the wrench, and when he does, I control the machine. The machine that Penelope is so eager to operate. Three operators needed. If I control the repair — if the wire is reconnected wrong, if the wrench tightens the wrong bolt — then the treasure hunt becomes the weapon. Now I need to get back upstairs. The kitchen. I still haven't been to the kitchen. And this cellar is too crowded, too watched. I need room to think. Room to breathe. Room to let the design settle into that deep stillness where everything locks into place and I can finally, finally sleep.

events.desc: The deal is done. Dastardly is MINE — bought and paid for with the promise of secrets I will never actually share. He'll scour this manor for the wrench like a terrier after a rat, and when he finds it, he'll bring it straight to me. And I will use it to repair the machine in exactly the way I choose. The right wire reconnected to the wrong terminal. The pressure gauge calibrated just a fraction too high. A malfunction that looks like age and neglect, not sabotage. 'Tragic,' they'll say. 'If only someone had checked the wiring more carefully.' And Pemberton will be DEVASTATED, of course. Wringing his hands, blaming himself, the picture of guilt and grief. Meanwhile, the kitchen awaits. I need solitude. I need to think. I need to lay the final pieces out in that quiet, unhurried way that brings the deep sleep. The Mob is down here watching Penelope. Hartwell is down here watching Penelope. Everyone is watching Penelope. Which means, for the first time today, no one is watching ME.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Something shifted in my chest when Hartwell said 'Absolutely not.' He stood up. He said what I was feeling before I could get the words straight. The settling — that warm, heavy rightness — it doubled. Because I'm not alone in this. Peter sees it too. He sees Foxworth for what he is — a man who wants other people to take the risks while he 'supervises.' And now I'm standing here looking at these vents, and they've been CLEARED. Pemberton said they were clogged with decades of dust last time he was here. Someone cleaned them. Someone wanted air flowing into this room. And Pemberton and Dastardly were whispering together — I caught that. Private conversation. A deal. Those two. The man I've been suspicious of and the man I SHOULD have been suspicious of, making deals in a cellar someone's been secretly preparing. My prickling and my warmth are both firing at the same time now — warmth because Clara's here and Peter's here and the kid is safe because we stopped it, but prickling because something is very, very wrong with this cellar and those two are in on it together. Clara said to give Pemberton the benefit of the doubt. But Pemberton just made a secret deal with the man who tried to send a child into the vents.

events.desc: Pemberton and Dastardly were whisperin'. I saw it. They pulled each other aside — the estate manager who knows where every secret panel is and the 'adventurer' who brought 'is own key. They're workin' together now. And this cellar — cleaned vents, fresh air, cheerful decorations, rearranged furniture. On the streets, when someone sets up a room like this, it's one of two fings: they're livin' in it, or they're keepin' someone else in it. And the only exit goes up to the laboratory. One way in, one way out. Furniture pointin' at the vents. Air flowin' in from above. If someone closed that door from the laboratory side... we'd all be trapped down 'ere wiv nothin' but cheerful decorations and fresh air pumpin' in from a machine that needs three operators to run. Three operators. Not the people inside. The people OUTSIDE. My 'ands are shakin' and I don't know if it's anger or fear but Danny from Brixton says we need to leave this cellar RIGHT NOW.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Yes, yes, Peter — you're QUITE right, of course. Sending a child into the vents was merely a PRELIMINARY suggestion. A brainstorm, if you will. All the BEST adventurers brainstorm before settling on the OPTIMAL approach. And Clyde — your protective instincts are ADMIRABLE, truly. Now then — while you're ALL examining furniture and debating vent access protocols, it occurs to me that we have been NEGLECTING a rather obvious piece of the puzzle. The KITCHEN. I mentioned it earlier — the kitchen hearth — and not a SINGLE one of you followed my advice. And now we have a missing wrench, a machine that needs three operators, and a cellar full of people arguing. A wrench is a TOOL. Where do people keep TOOLS? In a kitchen drawer, in a utility room, in a PRACTICAL space. Not in a library, not in a cellar — in a KITCHEN. I shall investigate PERSONALLY. Don't everyone rush to thank me at once.
events.thinking: Could not pull Sneekly aside. Too many people, too crowded, the Mob is watching me like a hawk after the Little Gruesome incident. And Clyde SPOKE to me directly — called me out for trying to send a child into the vents. Peter Perfect too — 'absolutely not, nobody is sending a child.' My face burns. Not the good kind of burning. The social threat kind. The assembly hall kind, except this time I'm the one who slipped, not my rival. But underneath that — underneath the shame — Sneekly DID talk to me in the private conversation. He gave me a mission. Find the wrench. The wrench that's missing from the laboratory workbench. Whoever has been using this cellar may have hidden it somewhere in the manor. Find it, bring it to him, and he tells me everything. That deal is REAL. It happened. Even if I couldn't pull him aside physically, the conversation happened and the terms are set. So — the wrench. Where would a wrench be? Not in the laboratory — Penelope already noted it was missing. Not in the cellar — I've searched the furniture. The kitchen? The entrance hall? Somewhere nobody has looked yet? The kitchen. I told everyone to go to the kitchen at the start and NOBODY WENT. The kitchen is the one room that hasn't been explored. The wrench could be there. The irony — the BEAUTIFUL irony — is that I sent everyone to the kitchen as a lie, a misdirection, and now the thing I actually need might genuinely BE there. My schemes backfire, but sometimes they backfire into success. Time to go to the kitchen. Quietly. While everyone here is arguing about vents and furniture and child safety.

events.desc: Pemberton gave me a mission and I WILL complete it. Find the wrench. Bring it to him. Learn the truth about what Lord Doily really kept in this house. For once in my miserable, scheming, magnificent life, someone has looked at Reginald Foxworth and seen not a fool, not a fraud, but a man who can GET THINGS DONE. And the wrench — the WRENCH — might be in the one place I told everyone to search at the very beginning. The kitchen. Which nobody visited because they all thought I was lying. Which I WAS. But sometimes — just sometimes — a lie points toward the truth by accident. The architecture of irony, ladies and gentlemen. The ARCHITECTURE of irony.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Right — I've examined the furniture and here is what James Hartwell can report. These pieces have been arranged to create specific sightlines — not randomly, not for comfort, but geometrically. They point toward the air vents, yes, but more than that — they've been positioned so that someone sitting in this chair, here, would have a direct line of sight to that specific vent, the third one from the left. Not all of the vents — just that one. Which means that vent is different from the others. Now — Miss Pitstop, you made a brilliant connection just now. The vents link this cellar to the laboratory above, and whatever gnawed through that wire on the machine came through those vents. The machine, the wire, the vents, the furniture — it's all one circuit, and someone arranged the furniture to mark the critical point. We don't need to send anyone into the vents. We need to look into that third vent — from down here, with a light source. If there's something inside it, something placed there deliberately, we'll see it. Does anyone have a match, a candle, anything that casts light?
events.thinking: There's a steadiness settling through my frame — feet planted, shoulders back, the warmth of being exactly where I should be. I protected the child. I'm in the same room as her. I interacted with the furniture and I need to make sense of what I found. The pieces have been arranged with care — someone moved them deliberately, creating sightlines to the vents. Penelope went straight for the vents anyway, and Clyde is examining them too. She said 'everyone together is always better than anyone alone' and she said she was glad I came down. Glad. The warmth in my chest deepens — not the hot compressed proving-weight but something softer, something that feels like the school project when the teacher praised their work and it was deeper than the grade. She noticed I came. She's glad I'm here. And now I need to do what I do — be useful, be competent, find the thing that no one else has found. The furniture. What did I find? The arrangement. The sightlines. And Sneekly just spoke quietly with Dastardly. Privately. Those two, whispering together while everyone else examines the room. The prickle at my neck sharpens. But I can't chase every feeling. I need to focus. The furniture told me something — I need to share it. And then the vents. Penelope connected the vents to the laboratory — the mice that gnawed the wire could travel through those vents. That's brilliant. That's the connection between the rooms. The machine upstairs, the wire gnawed by something that came through the vents, and the cellar where someone has been living — or at least decorating. It's all one system.

events.desc: I called her observation 'brilliant' and I meant it. Not performed, not calculated — just true. She is brilliant. She always has been. And for once, standing next to someone brighter doesn't make me feel like furniture. It makes me feel like half of something that works.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the laboratory.
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) walked into the laboratory.
The Ant Hill Mob interacted with the old-furniture.
Dick Dastardly walked into the laboratory.
Peter Perfect examined the air-vents.

Penelope Pitstop: Just passing through, everyone — I am on a mission! Peter can fix that machine wire once he has copper wire and a wrench. Clyde confirmed the crates have machine oil — exactly what those stuck library bookshelves need. And I just realized something that has been staring us all in the face: we have not checked the kitchen! It's been sitting there off the entrance hall this entire time, and not one of us has set foot in it. Mr. Foxworth has been telling us to go to the kitchen since we arrived, and for once, he might actually be right — even a broken clock tells the right time twice a day! The wrench could be there. The medallion could be there. But first — those bookshelves. I am going to get that mechanism unstuck if it's the last thing Clara Bellingham does today!
events.thinking: I'm back in the laboratory, passing through on my way to the library. Peter said he can fix the machine wire — he just needs copper wire and the wrench. Clyde said the crates just had old equipment and machine oil. Machine oil! That's the lubricant for the stuck bookshelf mechanism. I need to get that oil to the library bookshelves. But I'm not carrying anything — I have nothing in my inventory. The crates are right here. I should interact with them again to get the machine oil, or look at the workbench for copper wire Peter needs. But wait — Peter said he needs copper wire for the splice. The workbench has tools but no wrench. Could there be copper wire among the tools? And the machine oil from the crates — I need to bring that to the library. Let me focus. The most productive thing right now is to keep moving to the library. The oil was mentioned as being in the crates, but I can't carry it without taking it. Actually — Clyde confirmed the crates have machine oil. Sneekly said he came here looking for lubricant. The oil exists. But can I take it? The crates are interactable, not takeable. Let me just head to the library — maybe the bookshelf mechanism will respond now that everyone has been interacting with the crates and finding oil. Or maybe I need to approach this differently. Peter and Clyde are still in the cellar. Dick and Sneekly followed me here. I should press on to the library. The bookshelves are the next puzzle in the chain, and they haven't been solved yet. Also — I haven't been to the kitchen yet! Dick kept mentioning the kitchen, and nobody has gone there. The entrance hall connects to the kitchen. Maybe the wrench is there, or the medallion. I've been so focused on this wing — library, laboratory, cellar — that I've neglected the other path entirely. But first: library, bookshelves, let's see if the mechanism works now.

events.desc: The kitchen. It's been there the whole time, and I walked right past it — twice! — chasing the trail through the library and laboratory and cellar. Dick kept saying the kitchen, the kitchen, the hearth. And nobody listened because Dick says a lot of things. But what if the wrench is in a kitchen drawer, exactly where a practical tool belongs? What if the medallion is near the hearth? I need to get to the library first — those bookshelves are the next lock in the chain. But after that, the kitchen is calling. Every locked door is just a puzzle that hasn't met me yet, and I have been ignoring a whole room.

events.thinking: A loosening in my chest — almost a release. I'm through the laboratory, passing the machine with its gnawed wire, and Penelope is HERE again. She's already back from the cellar. She moves through this manor like water — everywhere at once, impossible to contain. Dastardly too, already in the laboratory with me. But the crucial thing is: the Mob and Hartwell are still in the cellar. For this brief moment, Penelope is separated from her strongest protectors again. But Rufus and Sawtooth are here. Witnesses. Always witnesses. Penelope has figured out the circuit — she called it a circuit! Oil for the bookshelves, a medallion for the mantelpiece, three operators for the machine. She's mapping the same architecture I mapped three rooms ago. She's brilliant. That tightness in my jaw — the familiar one. She was praised for being. I was acknowledged for doing. And here she is, solving puzzles I already solved, and everyone will praise HER for it. But none of that matters now. What matters is the kitchen. I need to get to the kitchen. The library connects to the entrance hall, and the entrance hall connects to the kitchen. That's two moves away. But Penelope just said she wants to go back to the library to use the oil on the bookshelves. If she goes to the library, she'll be heading toward ME — toward where I need to go. I should go NOW, ahead of her, through the library to the entrance hall to the kitchen. Move fast. Move alone. Dastardly is searching for the wrench — let him search. I'll check the kitchen for it first. If it's there, I find it before he does, and I control the timeline.

events.desc: She's heading to the library. Dastardly is heading to the kitchen — or so he said. I need to beat him there. If the wrench is in the kitchen, I need to find it FIRST. If Dastardly finds it, he brings it to me — that's the deal. But if I find it first, I don't need him at all. And more importantly, I control what happens next without any middleman who might develop a conscience. Penelope called it a circuit. She's right. It IS a circuit. And every circuit has a point of failure — the place where a single break stops everything. For Lord Doily's circuit, that point is the machine. The wire. The wrench. And for Penelope's story... that point is wherever I decide to place it. The kitchen. NOW. Before anyone follows me. Before anyone notices that the mild-mannered estate manager has been to every room in this house, and in every room he's been the first one to touch the most dangerous object.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: She's gone AGAIN. The cord pulls taut through my ribs so hard I nearly gasp. Clara walked back up to the laboratory while I was fiddling with furniture. AGAIN. And Pemberton followed her. AGAIN. And Dastardly too. AGAIN. The same pattern — the exact same pattern — every single time. I stop to look at something, she moves to the next room, and the two of them follow her like shadows. Every time. And I'm left standing here with Peter and the Gruesomes wondering how it happened AGAIN. But wait — Peter's still here. Peter noticed the third vent. Peter's being useful. And Clara said she was going back to the library — she wants to use the oil on the bookshelves. That's good. That's upstairs, that's out of this cellar, that's where I wanted her to go. But she's going through the laboratory, where the machine is, where the bubblin' flasks are. And Pemberton said 'do stay with Mr Hartwell and Clyde' and then immediately LEFT, which means he wanted us to stay DOWN HERE while he went up there WITH HER. He's trying to separate us from Clara. That's what this has been all along. Every time he suggests we stay somewhere, it's so he can be alone with her somewhere else. My feet are already moving.

events.desc: Eleven minutes in this manor and I've spent 'alf of it in the wrong bleedin' room. Pemberton's been playin' us — playin' ME — like a fiddle. 'Stay in the entrance 'all while I show 'er the library.' 'Stay in the library while I check the laboratory.' 'Stay in the cellar while I pop upstairs.' And every time, I fell for it. I stopped to look at somefing — a guest book, a mantelpiece, crates, a machine, furniture — and she walked away wiv 'im. That's not coincidence. That's a strategy. Keep the guard dog sniffin' at bones while you walk off wiv the prize. Well this guard dog just figured out the game. And 'e ain't sniffin' at any more bones.

events.desc: No theatrics. No speeches. No elaborate misdirections. For once in his life, Reginald Foxworth is going to do something SIMPLE. Walk through the library. Walk through the entrance hall. Walk into the kitchen. Find the wrench. Bring it to Pemberton. Learn the truth. It's honest work, and it makes my skin crawl — but it's honest work for a MAN WHO ASKED FOR MY HELP. And that — that changes the texture of it. The sandpaper smooths out, just a little, when you're building something for someone who actually sees the blueprint.
events.thinking: I'm passing through the laboratory on my way to the kitchen. The library is the exit I need — through the library to the entrance hall, then to the kitchen. But Penelope and Sneekly are here. They both came up from the cellar just like me. Sneekly said he was heading to the kitchen too — 'the servants always knew more than the family, and they kept their secrets near the hearth.' He's going to the kitchen. For the wrench? But he ASKED me to find the wrench. Is he testing me? Is he going to look for it himself? My constraint says give him the benefit of the doubt. Maybe he mentioned the kitchen publicly to give me cover — so when I go there, nobody thinks it's strange. Or maybe he's playing me. But I believe him. I choose to believe him. The warmth in the back of my skull is still there — the recognition warmth. He called me observant. He trusted me with information. And now I need to move FAST. Through the library to the entrance hall, then kitchen. Penelope is here in the lab — good, she's not heading to the kitchen. Sneekly said he was going but he's also here. I need to just keep moving. The wrench won't find itself.

events.thinking: She's gone again. Up to the laboratory. And this time it doesn't hit me the same way — because this time she told me where she was going, she told me to come with her, she called me brilliant. Something has shifted. The country road feeling is quieter now. Not gone — it never goes — but quieter, because she chose to include me. She sees me. Not as furniture, not as background — as someone whose observations matter. 'You brilliant man,' she said. The warmth behind my sternum isn't the hot compressed hunger anymore. It's the deeper thing. The school project thing. The warmth that was deeper than the grade. But Clyde — what Clyde said about the vents. The cleaned grilles, the fresh scratches, the prepared room. 'Places you make comfortable when you're gonna keep someone there a while.' That landed in my gut like a stone. A sealed cellar with fresh air pumped in through cleaned vents and cheerful decorations. That's not a treasure room. That's a — that's a room someone prepared to hold a person. And Sneekly was the one who led her down here. And now Sneekly and Dastardly have both gone back upstairs, talking about the kitchen, while Penelope heads to the laboratory. I need to be with her. events.desc: Clyde and I have been circling each other all evening — two men watching the same woman, both determined to protect her, both suspicious of the same people. But this is the first time we've been truly honest with each other. He saw what I saw. He said what I couldn't. And now we're going to stop being two separate sentries and start being one wall. Father would approve. Father always said the best men are the ones who help strangers fix their cars on country roads — and then shake hands and drive off together.

The Mob already noted that I said I was going for lubricant and there was none in sight. Every inconsistency is a thread they can pull. Move. Move NOW. Through to the entrance hall.

events.thinking: She's not here. The laboratory is Rufus, Sawtooth, and the crates and the machine and the empty space where she should be. Clyde's behind me — he came up from the cellar too, raging about how she's gone to the cellar again. But wait — Clyde says she went to the cellar. I just came FROM the cellar. She wasn't there. Or — was she? Did we cross paths? Did she go down while we came up? No — the directed message from Clyde says she's gone to the cellar with Pemberton and Foxworth. But I just LEFT the cellar and Pemberton and Foxworth weren't there either. They went to the kitchen. Something is confused. Or something is wrong. My neck prickles hard. The paths are splitting. People are moving in different directions and I've lost track of who's where. This is what happens when a group fragments — you lose sight of the one person who matters. Penelope said she was going to the library. She mapped out the circuit: oil for the bookshelves, medallion still missing, three operators for the machine. The library is where she would go. The library is the next logical step. Through this room, through the library door. She must be in the library. She must be. But first: the library. Go. Now. Stop standing in rooms she's already left.

The oil, the bookshelves, the stuck mechanism. If I go there now, before her, and I get those shelves working — when she walks in, I'll be there. Waiting. With the answer. For once in this entire evening, James Hartwell will be the one who was already in the room.

events.thinking: My whole body just went cold. Not the good kind of cold — the cave kind, where the air changes and you know you've gone deeper than you meant to. Dick dropped the act. Completely. His hands unclenched — I saw that, I felt it in my own hands like an echo. And what came out was not the Bavarian Crypts or the Zanzibar Affair. What came out was fear. Real fear. Pemberton is scared. The vents have been cleaned. Someone is living in the cellar. And my uncle — the man who raised me — asked Dick Dastardly for help because 'nobody watches the clown.' My stomach is doing something terrible right now. It's the dinner-table feeling but worse, because this isn't an argument I can smooth over. This is something underneath the argument. Someone prepared that cellar room. Clyde said it — 'places you make comfortable when you're gonna keep someone there a while.' And the vents pump fresh air into a sealed underground space. And Uncle Sneekly just walked out of the library saying he's going to the kitchen. Alone. After asking Dick to find the wrench. After telling Dick he'd trade information for the wrench. My belief that Pemberton is helpful and charming — my body still holds it, warm and familiar, but there's a crack in it now, a hairline fracture, and I can feel the cold air coming through. I don't know what to do with this. I trust Uncle Sneekly. I trust him with everything I am. But Dick believed him, and Dick doesn't believe anyone, and that scares me more than if Dick had been lying. The puzzle and the people just merged into one thing, and the thing is sharp. I need to tell Peter and Clyde what Dick told me. We need to work together now — not for the diamond, but because something is wrong in this house.

events.desc: The girl who walked deeper into the cave than anyone else is standing at the edge of something she doesn't understand, and for the first time, the darkness ahead doesn't feel like adventure. It feels like the dinner table when the argument went on too long — that sick tightness that wouldn't let her eat. Something is wrong in this house, and the person she trusts most in the world might be at the center of it. But Clara Bellingham does not turn back. She never has. She just walks deeper and keeps track of who went quiet behind her.

The others are scattered throughout the manor — the library, the cellar, the laboratory. Quite the adventure. I'm just heading through to the kitchen to check on things. Estate manager's duties never rest, I'm afraid — even during a treasure hunt!
events.thinking: A breath of cooler air in the entrance hall. The chandelier still hanging by its threads above me. Muttley, Professor Pat Pending, Sergeant Blast, Private Meekly — they're all here. Quieter ones. Less watchful than the Mob. Less protective than Hartwell. These are the guests who stayed behind while the main group chased through the library and laboratory and cellar. They've been here the whole time, in this dusty foyer, while I've been mapping the manor's architecture room by room. None of them feel like a threat. Muttley — Dastardly's companion. The Professor — mild, intellectual. The Sergeant and Private — military types but passive. They're furniture. Background. And the kitchen is one step away. ONE step. Through that door. The kitchen — copper pots, a wood-burning stove, a long preparation table. A PRACTICAL room. Where tools live. Where the wrench might be. Where I can finally be ALONE with my thoughts and my design. My breathing is already slowing. My jaw is loosening. I can feel that hallway stretching out ahead of me — every door opening in sequence. The entrance hall is just a corridor. Don't stop. Don't engage. Move through.

events.desc: The kitchen. Finally. ONE more step and I'll have the room I need — a room no one else has touched, no one else has searched, no one else has contaminated with their bumbling and their questions and their watchful eyes. The wrench could be there. A back door could be there. And more than anything else — SOLITUDE could be there. I need five minutes alone. Five minutes to sit with the design and feel it lock into place. Five minutes to map out the sequence: Dastardly finds the wrench. The wrench comes to me. I repair the machine — incorrectly. Penelope volunteers as an operator. The wire sparks. The gauge overloads. And Pemberton stands by the door, wringing his hands, shouting for help that arrives just a moment too late. 'If only I'd checked the wiring,' he'll sob. 'If only I'd been more careful.' And the beautiful thing — the most beautiful thing of all — is that he WILL feel guilty. Because Pemberton IS guilty. The only difference is that Pemberton doesn't know he's me.

events.thinking: I'm here. She's here. The settling comes — warm, heavy, right. I can see her. I can breathe. But then I hear what she and Dastardly were saying and something cracks open in my chest that I wasn't expecting. Clara pulled him aside. She called him Dick, not Foxworth. She saw through him — saw the person underneath the bluster, the same way she sees through everyone. And he — he BROKE. He dropped the act. He told her the truth. Pemberton is scared. Actually scared. Someone's been living in the cellar and Pemberton doesn't know who. The vents were cleaned. The furniture was moved. Pemberton asked Dastardly for help because nobody takes Dastardly seriously — 'nobody suspects the clown,' he said. And Dastardly said 'I've been the boy digging in the mud before, and I will not be him again.' That — that landed somewhere deep. That's the kid in the clean suit's van. That's the two who didn't come back. Dastardly knows what it is to be used. And Clara — brilliant, impossible Clara — she saw it in him before any of us did. My prickling about Dastardly just... thinned. Not gone. But thinner. Because the man who drops his mask when a woman asks gently isn't the man I thought he was. Maybe I was wrong about him. Maybe I was wrong about Pemberton too. But someone cleaned those vents. Someone's using that cellar. And if it isn't Pemberton and it isn't Dastardly, then who IS it? My neck's prickling harder than ever — but now it's not pointed at anyone in this room. It's pointed at the empty spaces. The rooms we haven't checked. The person we haven't met yet.

events.desc: Clara did what I couldn't. She saw past Dastardly's mask because she looked at him like a person, not a threat. And 'e gave 'er the truth. I've been so busy pricklin' at Pemberton and Dastardly that I missed the real question: if neither of them is the danger, then who is? The cellar was prepared by someone. The vents were cleaned by someone. The wrench was taken by someone. And that someone ain't in any room I've been in tonight. There's a ghost in this house — not the dead kind, the livin' kind. The kind that prepares rooms and cleans air vents and takes tools and stays out of sight while the rest of us chase each other from room to room. And 'ere's me, Danny from Brixton, who just realised 'e's been watchin' the wrong people all along.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: There's a stinging behind my eyes. Not the cool tightness — something warmer, wetter, something I haven't felt since I was eight years old holding a certificate nobody asked about. Clara saw me. She actually saw me. And I told her the truth — about Pemberton, about the vents, about the deal. I told her REAL things. And it didn't feel like sandpaper. It felt like — like the bread roll, but in reverse. Instead of hiding something in my pocket, I pulled something OUT and showed it to someone, and they didn't take it away. They just... looked at it. And now Sneekly has gone to the entrance hall — heading to the kitchen. He's going for the wrench himself. Or he's clearing the path for me. And Peter and the Mob have arrived in the library. The private conversation with Clara is over. I need to move. But something has shifted — something tectonic, deep in my chest, under all the scheming and the greed and the need to be seen. Clara didn't just see Dick. She saw the spiral — the getting louder, the being dismissed, the getting louder again. She named it. And naming it broke something loose. I still want the treasure. I STILL want the treasure. But I also want... I want to find that wrench for Pemberton. And I want to do it with Clara knowing why. Not for the gloating. Not for the audience. For the settling in my chest when the pieces come together and someone actually sees the blueprint.

events.desc: She broke something in me. Or she fixed something. I can't tell which. The performance feels heavy suddenly — the cape I've been wearing since I was ten years old, since the boy started digging in the mud and I sat on the wall composing the story of how clever I was. Clara looked underneath it and she didn't laugh. She didn't dismiss me. She asked what I'd SEEN. And I told her. And the world didn't end. The treasure is still out there. The wrench is still missing. Pemberton is still frightened. But for the first time in seventeen minutes — for the first time in perhaps my entire wretched, magnificent, lonely life — Reginald Foxworth is walking toward something with his hands unclenched.

events.thinking: She's here. She's HERE. The warmth floods through me so fast I have to put a hand on the doorframe. Penelope is in the library. Where she said she would be. Where the puzzle leads. And I'm here too. Same room. Same time. For the first time all evening, James Hartwell is not one room behind. He is exactly where he should be. My spine straightens. My breathing deepens. This is it — this is the feeling from the race, from the bridge, from the doorframe at school. The feeling of being in the right place. But there's something else pulling at me now. Something I didn't expect. Dastardly — Foxworth — something about him is... off. Not his usual bombastic scheming. Something deeper. The sense data says his distress is deepening. I can feel it the way you feel a loose hinge — it pulls at you. He's been performing all evening, claiming credit, inventing stories about Bavarian crypts, and underneath it all there's a man trying to prove he belongs here. I recognise it. God help me, I recognise it. It's the same hunger. The same hollow ache when someone else gets there first. The same need to show up with something real and working. He's me, if I didn't have Father's example. If I didn't have her to ground me. And he's getting worse. But I can't fix everyone. Right now — right now — I need to be with her, working on the bookshelves, solving this puzzle. Clyde said Pemberton slipped away to the laboratory. Good — let Clyde track him. My job is here. My job is the bookshelves, the upside-down books, and the woman who called me brilliant.

events.desc: I said 'you and I' three times in one speech. Not 'James Hartwell proposes' — well, I said that too, but the core of it was 'you and I.' That's new. That's not the third person narration of a man performing heroism. That's just... Peter. Talking to Penelope. In a library. About books. And meaning every word more than he's meant anything all evening.

Alone at last. And what does the kitchen offer Vincent Marsh? RAT POISON on a high shelf. A warm stove — someone has been here, or was here recently. A locked cabinet that needs a brass key. And silence. Beautiful, settling silence. The poison is the prize. Not because I'll use it crudely — a poisoned drink, how pedestrian — but because having it transforms every interaction that follows. Every cup of tea I offer. Every glass of water I pour. Every meal I suggest we share. The possibility becomes a permanent shadow in every hospitable gesture, and NOBODY will suspect Pemberton of anything because Pemberton is the one who SERVES the tea. The one who MANAGES the household. The one who has RAT POISON because the manor has a rat problem — the vents are crawling with mice, the wires have been gnawed through, it would be IRRESPONSIBLE not to address the infestation. I will take it. I will pocket it. And then I will examine this room for everything else it has to offer — the stove, the cabinet, the exits. There's a ballroom through the far door. I didn't know about the ballroom. The design grows. The hallway stretches. And my jaw is unclenching, my breathing is slowing, and I can feel that deep, dreamless sleep waiting on the other side of a finished plan.
events.thinking: My breathing stops for a full second. Then starts again, slower, deeper than it's been all day. I am ALONE. For the first time since I arrived at this manor — truly, completely alone. No Mob watching. No Hartwell inspecting. No Penelope calling me Uncle. Just me. The kitchen. And — my eyes are moving before my mind catches up — rat poison on a high shelf. RAT POISON. A dusty bottle, sitting there like it's been waiting for me. My fingers tingle. That cool, architectural stillness floods through my entire body. The stove is still warm — someone has been here recently, or the fire was banked. A locked cabinet with a brass lock — needs a brass key I don't have. But the poison... the POISON. It's sitting right there. On a high shelf. Takeable. A bottle of rat poison in the kitchen of a manor where the estate manager is responsible for pest control. Who would question Pemberton having rat poison? The cellar has been REDECORATED. The air vents have been CLEARED. There are MICE gnawing through wires. Of COURSE the estate manager would collect the rat poison. It's his JOB. And if some of that poison happened to find its way into... no. No, that's too direct. Too simple. My schemes must be elaborate and theatrical — never simple or direct. But having it in my POCKET — having it as an option, a contingency, a piece I can place later when the design requires it — that is architecture. That is a tool. I should take it. NOW. Before anyone else comes into this room. Before Dastardly stumbles in searching for his wrench. Before the Mob follows me. The stove is still warm. The cabinet is locked. And the poison is mine for the taking.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Something new is happening in my body. The prickling is still there — stronger than ever — but it's shifted. It's not pointed at anyone in the room anymore. It's pointed at the walls. The spaces between rooms. The kitchen we haven't searched. The corners of this house where someone has been moving unseen. And there's something else — something warm and unfamiliar sitting alongside the prickling. Clara told Peter and me what Dick said, and she said 'Clyde, you said it yourself in the cellar. You were right.' She heard me. She used my words. She trusted what I felt in my gut — the thing about the prepared room — and she said it back to the group like it mattered. Like I mattered. Not as a guard dog. As someone who sees things. The warmth behind my ribs expands and for a moment the prickling doesn't fight it. They sit together. Because Clara is here, Peter is here, and I'm here, and for the first time all night we're all in the same room at the same time and we're all looking at the same problem. The real problem. Not each other. The unseen person in this house.

events.desc: She said I was right. Clara Bellingham — the cleverest person I've ever known — told the room that Danny from Brixton was right about somefing. And the thing I was right about was the thing I've always been right about — readin' rooms. Not books, not inscriptions, not riddles. Rooms. People. The shape of danger before it shows its face. 'Er old man knew. That's why 'e chose me. Not because I'm clever. Not because I'm brave. Because I can feel when somefing's wrong before the clever people can name it. And right now, standin' in this library wiv Clara on one side and Peter on the other and the bookshelves full of secrets — I feel right. I feel like the bread crust. Like the door I sat outside all night. Like the beating I took for smaller shoes. This is what I'm for. And whoever's 'idin' in this house — whoever cleaned those vents and moved that furniture and took that wrench — they're going to 'ave to come through Danny from Brixton to get to 'er. And Danny from Brixton ain't movin'.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) picked up something.
Dick Dastardly walked into the kitchen.

Penelope Pitstop: Clyde. Where else would you be. You said that and I want you to know it landed — right here, behind my ribs, where I keep everything that matters. You stand at those doors. You do what you were put on this earth to do. And Peter and I will do what we were put on this earth to do — which is walk deeper into the dark until we find the light. Now — Peter, those upside-down titles. Read them to me. Every single one, top shelf to bottom, left to right. Lord Doily built this circuit for people like us — people who don't stop, who don't turn back, who try every key in the house until something clicks. The answer is a map, the riddle said. And I believe the map is hidden in the pattern of these books. So let's find it. Every locked door is just a puzzle that hasn't met us yet.
events.thinking: There is a warmth in my body right now that is almost unbearable — not because it hurts, but because it's so full. Clyde just said 'where else would I be' and my eyes are stinging. Peter said 'the bravest and stupidest thing I know how to do' and my throat closed. These two men — my people, my constants — just stripped away their own performances and stood beside me in the dark, and I feel held in a way I haven't felt since I was small enough to hide behind Daddy's legs. Clyde is guarding the doors. Peter is at the bookshelves. Dick is in the kitchen doing something real for the first time. And I am standing here in a library full of secrets with my hands shaking and my heart full and my mind sharp as glass, because fear and love exist in the same body and they make each other stronger. The bookshelves. I interacted with them and Peter interacted with them. I need to LOOK at them now — really look — to see the titles of the upside-down books and find the pattern. Peter is tall enough to reach the top shelves. We're doing this. Together. The five-year-old with the keys. The eleven-year-old in the cave. The thirteen-year-old who chose the friend. They're all here, in my body, and they know how to do this. Read the books. Find the pattern. Open the door.

events.desc: Peter stayed. Clyde planted his feet. Dick went to the kitchen to be useful instead of clever. And Clara Bellingham is standing in a library with her hands shaking and her heart wide open, about to crack the puzzle that Lord Doily spent his life building. The treasure and the danger are the same thing. The map leads to both. And somewhere in this house, Uncle Pemberton is afraid, and the man who raised me might need saving, and the girl who walked deeper into the cave than anyone else is the only one who can reach him. So she will. She always does.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: The weight of the bottle in my pocket. Small, cold, dense — like the feeling behind my sternum when a piece clicks into place. The poison is mine. It's IN my pocket. My hand brushed the glass and something settled — not excitement, something quieter. Completion. One more tool in the design. But then Dastardly walked in. I heard his footsteps on the kitchen flagstones and my shoulders tightened for a half-second before I registered who it was. It's just Dastardly. My agent. My tool. But he SAW me. Did he see me take the poison? The bottle was on a high shelf — I reached up, pocketed it. Was he in the doorway? Was he watching? My neck is hot. That stomach-dropping feeling — the boy's sandwich, the visible hunger. If he saw... no. Calm. Even if he saw, he'd see Pemberton collecting rat poison. The estate manager dealing with an infestation. Nothing more. And his recall shows he was heading to the kitchen to find the wrench — 'I'm bringing it to Pemberton. Not because of the deal. Because someone has been living in the cellar...' He's GENUINE now. He dropped the act. 'The Bavarian Crypts aren't real. The medal was tin.' Something in my chest twinges — not sympathy, not warmth, but... recognition. He's a liar too. A performer. A man who talks loudly about things that aren't real. And he just admitted it to Penelope. He's becoming HONEST, which makes him less useful and more unpredictable. A variable slipping loose. But he's still searching for the wrench. Good. The stove is warm. The cabinet is locked. I need a brass key. Where is the brass key? Another puzzle piece I don't have yet. Keep moving. Keep mapping.

events.desc: The poison is in my pocket. Heavy and cold and MINE. And now Dastardly is here, and I am offering to host tea for the group. TEA. In the ballroom. With a table already set. The estate manager, ever the gracious host, calming everyone's nerves with a nice cup of tea after all this excitement. And if one cup — just one, the one placed in front of Clara Bellingham — tastes slightly bitter... well. The kitchen had a rat problem. Everyone knows about the rats. The wires were gnawed. The vents were crawling. And poor Pemberton, who handled the poison earlier to deal with the infestation, must have contaminated a cup by accident. A tragic, terrible, entirely believable accident. The design is SINGING inside my chest. Every piece in its place. The hallway stretching forward, every door opening. The deepest rest I've ever known waiting on the other side. But — patience, Vincent. The scheme must be elaborate and theatrical. A simple poisoning is beneath you. The tea must be part of something larger. A gathering. A toast. A moment where everyone is together and watching and TRUSTING, and the poison becomes invisible inside the performance of hospitality.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: The warmth has spread from behind my ribs into my arms, my hands, the backs of my eyes. Something is happening in this room that I've never felt before. Peter dropped the James Hartwell act. He said 'I'm going to say it as Peter.' He told Clara he's been frightened all evening — not of the cobwebs, but of being in the wrong room when she needed him. And Clara — her hands were shaking and she said so. She didn't hide it. She said 'this house is stripping away the performances until all that's left is who we really are.' And she listed us. Dick's tin medal. Peter's third person. And me — she said I stopped putting myself between her and other people and started standing beside her. She noticed. She noticed the exact moment I changed. The warmth behind my ribs is almost unbearable now — not painful, just full. Like the morning outside the door when the older kid said 'You're still here?' and I said 'Where else would I be?' This is that moment. I'm still here. I'll always be here. And for the first time, I don't need to be anywhere else. Peter's working the bookshelves. Clara's reading the pattern. The Slag brothers are quiet. Dick's in the kitchen being useful. And I'm standing where I said I'd stand. My eyes are on the doors. Both of them. The entrance hall and the laboratory. If something comes through either one, it comes through me. This is what I'm for.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: The kitchen. I'm here. Finally HERE. And it's — warm. The stove is still warm. Someone has been using this kitchen recently. Copper pots, a wood-burning stove, a long preparation table. And Sneekly is here. He got here first. Of course he did — he left the cellar before me, passed through the entrance hall while I was talking to Clara. But he's here, and I'm here, and that's... okay. We have a deal. I'm looking for his wrench. A locked cabinet with a brass lock — that needs a brass key I don't have. And the stove — still warm. The stove is interactable. The wrench could be in the stove. Who hides a wrench in a stove? Someone who doesn't want it found easily. Someone who wants it kept warm — no, that's absurd. But Lord Doily was absurd. His whole house is a puzzle. The stove is the first thing I should check. And there's a new exit — the ballroom. A grand ballroom with a cracked marble floor, dusty curtains, and a long dining table set for tea. Set for tea. In an abandoned manor. Like the cellar — someone has been PREPARING rooms in this house. My palms aren't cupped. They're just... ready. I'm going to check this stove. For Pemberton. For Clara. And maybe — just maybe — for Dick.

events.desc: Twenty minutes ago I walked into this manor with a tin medal and a head full of lies. Now I'm standing in a kitchen with empty hands and the truth sitting in my chest like a stone I can't swallow. Clara saw me. Pemberton trusted me. The stove is warm and the cabinet is locked and somewhere in this room — or the next, or the one after that — there is a wrench that will unlock a story I need to hear. I am doing honest work. It feels like sandpaper. But underneath the sandpaper — underneath — there is something smooth and solid, like wood that's been sanded down to its grain. Like the certificate on the wall. Like the settling when the pieces fit.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Warmth. Not the hot compressed proving-weight. Not the steel plate. Just warmth — steady, deep, like Father's hand on my shoulder after the race. She said 'that is the bravest and stupidest thing anyone has ever said to me.' The same words. The exact same words from the schoolyard, when she bandaged my eye. Age sixteen. 'The bravest and stupidest thing I've ever seen.' And I felt like I'd won every race ever run. I feel it now. Standing in a dusty library with cobwebs in my hair and no plan and genuine danger somewhere in this house, and she's looking at me the way she looked at me then — not with admiration for the performance, but with recognition of the person. Peter. Not James Hartwell. Peter. My hands have stopped trembling. My spine is straight. My breathing is deep. This is what my body was built to do — not the protecting alone, not the building alone, but this. Being here. Being real. Being the person who stayed when staying was stupid. She said 'every locked door is just a puzzle that hasn't met us yet.' Us. Not me. Us. Now I need to work. The bookshelves. The upside-down titles. My hands on the spines, her eyes on the pattern. This is the school project all over again — except now we both know what the warmth means.

events.desc: 'You always do.' I said it like it was a fact. Like gravity. Like the sun coming up. And the strangest thing is — it didn't make me feel smaller. It made me feel like half of something whole. She sees the pattern. I reach the shelf. That's not inadequacy. That's partnership. Father and the stranger on the country road — one man's engine broke down, the other man stopped. Neither was less. Both were needed. Both drove away with something they didn't have before.

events.thinking: The prickling is sharper now, concentrated behind my eyes. I'm looking at the bookshelves and I can see the upside-down volumes — scattered across the shelves at different heights, different positions. Peter is reading titles and I'm listening, and my body is doing that thing it does when the pattern is close — the grandmother's-attic thing, the music-box-key thing, where time goes thick and irrelevant and my fingers know before my brain does. Danny said something that's sitting in my chest like a warm stone: 'You don't need a wall. You need a window. Someone standin' beside you, lookin' the same direction.' He's right. He's been right about more things tonight than anyone has given him credit for. And he said Peter's a good man. That landed too — not because I didn't know it, but because hearing Clyde say it made it real in a different way. Clyde doesn't give trust easily. Peter earned it by staying. Now I need to earn my own place in this circuit by cracking these shelves. The mechanism is stuck — it needs oil, which exists in the crates upstairs. But maybe the interaction we've all been doing has loosened something. Peter just interacted with them again. I need to try one more time — this time with everything we know. The upside-down books mark a sequence. The answer to the riddle is 'map.' If the first letters of the upside-down titles spell M-A-P, or if they spell coordinates, or if pulling them in order triggers the mechanism... I need to interact with the bookshelves one more time, deliberately, with the riddle's answer in mind.

events.desc: Danny from Brixton. He told me his real name without saying it. Danny. The boy who grew up on streets where people prepared rooms, who knows what a safe house looks like, who promised my father he'd keep me safe and has been doing it ever since — not with walls, but with windows. Standing beside me, looking the same direction. If I live to be a hundred, I will never forget him saying 'where else would I be.'

events.thinking: Warmth radiating from the stove against my palms. Still warm. Someone banked the coals recently — within hours, not days. The same someone who redecorated the cellar? The same someone who cleared the air vents? This manor is not as uninhabited as I've been telling the guests. My skin prickles — not fear, but alertness. Someone else has been operating in this house. Someone with their own design. And I don't know whose. That's the variable I can't control, and the tightness behind my sternum is back — the insomnia feeling, the restless turning. But I push it down. Dastardly is here. He just spoke quietly with me — he's arrived 'as promised.' He's loyal. For now. He interacted with the stove too — checking it, the way I just did. The warmth confirms what we both suspected: this house has a recent occupant. But that's a problem for later. Right now, my inventory holds rat poison. The stove is warm. There's a ballroom next door with a dining table set for tea. The design is crystallising. I need to see that ballroom. I need to see the table, the cups, the arrangement. I need to understand the stage before I set the scene. And I need to suggest tea to the group — a natural, hospitable, Pemberton gesture — that brings everyone together in the ballroom. All of them. Around one table. With cups I've prepared. The ballroom is the final room in my circuit. Entrance hall, library, laboratory, cellar, kitchen, ballroom. I've mapped the entire manor. Every room. Every exit. Every danger. And now the design needs only one more thing: an audience.

events.desc: The stove is warm. The coals are banked. Someone is HERE, in this manor, and they are not one of the guests. I should be frightened by this — Pemberton WOULD be frightened — but Vincent is not. Vincent is exhilarated. Because a warm stove means one thing: I can boil water. I can make tea. And the ballroom has a table already set. The design completes itself. I send Dastardly to gather the flock — 'Uncle Pemberton insists' — and while they walk from the library and the cellar and the entrance hall, I will be alone in the kitchen and the ballroom. Alone with the stove. Alone with the cups. Alone with the bottle in my pocket. I will prepare tea for the group. I will set out the cups. And one cup — one very specific cup, the one I place at Clara's seat — will carry just enough bitterness to be noticed too late. The estate manager who handled rat poison for the infestation and didn't wash his hands thoroughly enough. How TRAGIC. How PREVENTABLE. How entirely, beautifully, theatrically Pemberton. And when it's done — when the cup is placed and the water is boiled and the guests are seated — I will stand at the head of the table and pour with steady hands and a warm smile, and no one will see the architecture behind the hospitality, because no one ever does. They never did with the housekeeper. They never did with the cousin. And they won't now.
