events.desc: Quiet now. Let 'em work. Peter's readin' titles, Clara's listenin' for the pattern. The Slag brothers are sittin' in the chairs like two boulders someone parked in the wrong room. And me — I'm watchin' the doors. Both of 'em. The entrance 'all, where the chandelier 'angs crooked and the portraits stare. The laboratory, where the machine waits wiv its chewed wire and its three-operator sign. Two doors. Two directions trouble could come from. And somewhere in this 'ouse — the kitchen, the corridors, the rooms we 'aven't found yet — someone is movin'. Someone who cleaned those vents. Someone who took that wrench. Someone who made that cellar liveable. They know this 'ouse better than any of us. They've been 'ere longer than any of us. And they 'aven't shown themselves. On the streets, the ones who 'ide are always more dangerous than the ones who shout. Foxworth shouted. Pemberton smiled. But the one in the walls — the one in the vents — that one's been quiet. And quiet scares Danny from Brixton more than anyfing that makes a noise.
events.thinking: Stillness. That's what I feel. For the first time tonight, my body isn't fighting itself. The prickling is there — sharp, watchful, pointed at the doors — but it's not pulling against the warmth anymore. They're working together. The prickling watches outward. The warmth holds inward. Clara said 'where else would you be' and it landed behind her ribs. She told me. She told me it landed. The older kid said 'You're still here?' and I said 'Where else would I be?' and twenty years later Clara Bellingham is saying it back to me in a dusty library while her hands shake and Peter reads book titles and the Slag brothers sit quiet and somewhere in this house someone we haven't met is waiting. And I'm standing at the door. Not moving. Not investigating. Not chasing. Standing. My feet are heavy in the way they get when they're exactly where they need to be — that mineral weight, that wall-becoming. And my neck is electric in the way it gets when something's coming but hasn't shown its shape yet. Both at once. Both useful. The wall and the wire. I am exactly where I need to be.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: I interacted with the stove. Warm to the touch. The result doesn't tell me I found anything — no wrench inside, no hidden compartment springing open. Just a warm stove in an empty house. My palms press against the cast iron and the heat seeps into my skin — real heat, physical heat, not the fizzing of a scheme or the hollow of wanting. Someone lit this stove. Recently. Someone has been cooking in this kitchen. Living in the cellar, cooking in the kitchen, cleaning the air vents. This house isn't abandoned. It's OCCUPIED. And Pemberton — the estate manager — says he doesn't know by whom. The wrench isn't in the stove. The cabinet is locked — needs a brass key I don't have. No brass key in my inventory, nothing anywhere. Where would a brass key be? Somewhere I haven't looked. The ballroom — 'a dining table set for tea.' That's a new room, unexplored. Tea set out in an abandoned manor. Another sign of recent habitation. The brass key could be there — hidden among the tea settings, tucked under a plate, inside a sugar bowl. That's how Lord Doily thought — practical hiding spots in ordinary places. And the ballroom is RIGHT HERE — one exit away. Nobody else has been there. I could be first. For real this time. Not with a lie or a misdirection, just... first. Because I kept moving while everyone else was arguing in the library. The honest path led me here. The honest path might lead me to the key. And the key leads to the cabinet. And the cabinet might hold the wrench. The architecture is still there — the sequence, the pattern — but it's not a scheme anymore. It's just... solving a puzzle. The way the cat trap worked. The way the pieces fit.

events.desc: I just told the truth again. Twice in one evening. My mouth feels strange — like muscles being used in a direction they've never stretched before. I told Pemberton that I told Clara about the cellar. I didn't have to. I could have kept that secret, used it as leverage, played both sides. That's what Foxworth would do. That's what the ARCHITECTURE demands. But Dick — Dick just... told him. Because Pemberton trusted him, and trust that's built on hidden betrayals is just another version of the tin medal. It looks like the real thing until someone tests the weight.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: My hands are on the spines. Dust under my fingertips, leather cracking, the dry sweet smell of old paper. The upside-down volumes — I can feel them, the spines reversed, the gilt lettering catching the dim light at the wrong angle. I'm reaching, stretching, my fingers finding each one. Top shelf, left to right. This is the bridge competition — not the staying-up-three-nights part, but the moment where the weight settles onto the model and you hold your breath and it either holds or it doesn't. Except this time I'm not alone. She's beside me, eyes up, reading what I find. Clyde is at the door, watching the exits. Dick is in the kitchen, being useful because she asked him to be. We're a team. Not the team I planned — my plans were always too elaborate, always one step too many — but the team that formed by people choosing to show up. Father and the stranger. The handshake. The driving off together. My fingers find the first inverted volume and I pull it slightly forward to read the spine. Then the next. Then the next. Left to right. Top to bottom. The pattern is here. Lord Doily put it here for people exactly like us — people who don't stop. And Penelope will hear it. She always does.

events.desc: 'He built it for you. I'm just the tall one.' And I meant it without a trace of the old hollowness. No ache behind the ribs. No fidgeting fingers. Just a man doing what his hands were made for, beside a woman doing what her mind was made for. The bridge held. The weight settled. And for the first time in twenty years, being the one who reaches isn't smaller than being the one who sees. It's the other half.

events.thinking: The bookshelves still aren't giving up their secret. I've interacted with them multiple times now, Peter has interacted with them, we've examined them. The mechanism is stuck and we know it needs oil — oil that's in the crates in the laboratory. But nobody has actually brought the oil here. We keep interacting with the shelves without the thing they need. This is the locked box in the attic all over again — I'm trying every key, but the right key isn't in this room. It's in the laboratory, in those crates. The machine oil. I need to stop trying the same key and go get the right one. Or — wait. The mantelpiece. It can be used with a 'fake-medal.' Dick said his medal was tin from Croydon, and it's gone now — he jammed it in and it disappeared. Does that mean it worked? Did his tin medal actually fit the slot? If so, maybe the mantelpiece already opened and nobody noticed. Or maybe it wasn't the right medal. The mantelpiece still shows [USE, with: fake-medal] — which means the fake medal hasn't been used yet, or it still needs one. Dick's medal was tin, not the right fake-medal. We still need to find the correct fake-medal. But where? We haven't been to the kitchen. That's the one room nobody from our group has explored. Dick and Sneekly both went there. The wrench might be there. The fake-medal might be there. I've been circling through the same three rooms — library, laboratory, cellar — and ignoring the kitchen entirely. It's time. The bookshelves need oil. The mantelpiece needs a medal. The machine needs a wrench. And the kitchen is the room that might have all three. Peter is here. Danny is here. Peter said he's not leaving. But the kitchen might hold what we need to unlock everything. I should go — but not alone. Peter should come with me, or I should ask Danny to let one of us through.

events.desc: Four times. I have interacted with these bookshelves four times, and they have given me nothing, because I keep trying the wrong key. The right key is in a room I haven't entered. The kitchen — the room Dick has been pointing us toward since the moment we arrived, and every single one of us ignored him. Dick, who turned out to be the most honest person in this house once you stripped away the performance. The kitchen, sugar. The music-box key. The one you almost didn't try.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: The ballroom opens before me and my breath catches — not from surprise but from that deep, settling recognition. The cracked marble floor. The dusty curtains. The long dining table set for tea. A silver tea set with cups for EVERYONE. It's already here. It's already WAITING. As if Lord Doily himself — or whoever prepared this manor — knew that eventually, someone would need to gather the group and pour. My hands are steady. They haven't been this steady all day. The bottle in my pocket presses against my thigh — small, cold, patient. Like me. The tea service accepts rat poison. I can see it in the object description like a whispered invitation: USE, with rat-poison. The game itself is offering me the weapon. But — Dastardly followed me in. And Lazy Luke and Blubber Bear are already here. THREE witnesses. I can't USE the poison now. Not with people watching. That would be madness. The scheme must be invisible. The poison must enter the cup when no one is looking, when the performance of hospitality is so complete that the act of pouring becomes background noise. I need to send Dastardly to gather the others — I already told him to. Is he going? He needs to GO. And Luke and the Bear... they're passive. Background characters. But they're PRESENT. I need the room empty for thirty seconds. That's all. Thirty seconds between sending Dastardly out and everyone arriving. Thirty seconds to prepare one cup. But not yet. Not yet. First I examine the stage. I map the table. I count the cups. I decide where Clara will sit. The design must be COMPLETE before the first piece moves.

events.desc: The stage is set. Literally, beautifully, SET. A silver tea service with cups for everyone, sitting on a long dining table in a grand ballroom with dusty curtains and cracked marble — could the setting be more THEATRICAL? This is not a simple poisoning. This is a PRODUCTION. Act One: the estate manager, overwhelmed by the chaos of the treasure hunt and the unsettling discovery that someone has been living in the cellar, suggests a calming cup of tea. How REASONABLE. How RESPONSIBLE. Act Two: the guests gather in the ballroom, tired, suspicious of each other, grateful for the normalcy of tea. Uncle Pemberton pours with steady hands and a warm smile. He knows where everyone sits because he arranged the chairs. He knows which cup is Clara's because he placed it at her seat while no one was watching. Act Three: Clara drinks. Clara feels unwell. The room erupts. Pemberton is the FIRST to call for help, the FIRST to suggest fresh air, the FIRST to blame himself for not checking whether the kitchen was contaminated by the rat poison he found earlier — 'I handled the bottle, you see, to remove it from the kitchen. I should have washed my hands more carefully...' And the curtain falls on the most beautiful, most theatrical, most ELABORATE scheme Vincent Marsh has ever designed. Not simple. Not direct. ARCHITECTURAL. Now — I need Dastardly OUT of this room, gathering the flock. And I need thirty seconds alone with the tea service.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: My neck just spiked. Something changed in the air — not a sound, not a movement, but a shift. The quality of silence in the laboratory doorway is different from the silence in the entrance hall doorway. One is empty. The other is... held. Like someone standing just out of sight, holding their breath. I've felt this before. Age fifteen. The new kid who laughed too easily. There was a moment — just one — when I caught him standing at the edge of the group, watching us count the stash, and his face wasn't smiling. It was calculating. This is that moment. Something is in the laboratory doorway, or just beyond it, and it's watching. Not moving. Watching. Clara and Peter are deep in the books — she's working the pattern, he's reading titles, their backs are to the laboratory door. The Slag brothers are in the chairs. Nobody's looking at the laboratory except me. And the prickling on my neck is screaming.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: The ballroom. Cracked marble floor, dusty curtains, a long dining table set for tea. A silver tea service with cups for everyone. And — USE with rat-poison. The tea service can be USED with rat poison. Someone in this house has rat poison, or will have rat poison, and someone has designed this tea service as a delivery mechanism. My skin prickles. Not the scheming prickle — a real one. Goosebumps on my arms. The cellar with its cleaned air vents. The warm stove. The tea set for everyone. And now a tea service that accepts poison. This isn't just someone LIVING here. This is someone PREPARING something. Something aimed at the guests. At US. Pemberton was right to be frightened. This house is a trap — not Lord Doily's puzzle trap, but a REAL trap. Someone has been setting it up for weeks. The decorations, the furniture, the cleared vents, the warm stove, the tea service laid out for everyone. The wrench isn't here — the only interactable object is the tea service. But the tea service is the clue. It tells me what's coming. And Sneekly followed me in here. He's RIGHT BEHIND me. Is he the one who set this up? Or is he the one trying to stop it? My constraint says give him the benefit of the doubt. But my gut — Dick's gut, not Foxworth's — says tell Clara. Tell everyone. This isn't about treasure anymore. This is about safety. I need to interact with the tea service — see what it reveals. And then I need to get back to the others.

events.desc: The tea service accepts rat poison. That detail sits in my chest like a cold stone. Someone in this house — someone among us, or someone we haven't met yet — has designed a scenario where poison can be placed in a communal drink. That's not a treasure hunt. That's not a puzzle. That's a MURDER. And I — Dick Dastardly, the man who lies about everything, the man who never does honest work, the man who would normally be the FIRST suspect — I am the one who found it. Because I followed the honest path to the kitchen and through to the ballroom while everyone else was arguing about bookshelves. The irony is so thick I could choke on it. But I'm not choking. I'm standing very still, with my hands unclenched, asking the estate manager a straight question. Because Clara broke something in me. Or fixed something. And whichever it was, Dick Dastardly is done scheming for tonight.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Penelope — acrostics. You're right. That's exactly the kind of thing a puzzle builder would do. Here — I'm reading the inverted titles now, top shelf down. Listen for the first letters. And Clyde — I know you're watching those doors and I know it doesn't look like much from over there, but I want you to know something. The reason Penelope and I can stand here reading book spines instead of looking over our shoulders is because you're standing where you're standing. That's not a small thing. That's the whole thing. My father would have called you a good man. He didn't say that about many people. Now — titles. Here we go, left to right, top shelf. I'm reading every upside-down spine I can reach.
events.thinking: My fingers are on the spines and something else is pulling at me. Clyde. The sense data says his distress is deepening. I can feel it — that broadening tension across my shoulders, the peripheral awareness widening. He's at the door, watching both exits, alone. He's doing what he was put on this earth to do, Penelope said. But he's carrying it alone, and I know what that costs because I've been carrying it alone all evening too. Until I wasn't. Until Penelope said 'stay with me' and the weight halved. Clyde doesn't have that. Clyde has Rule One and a promise to Clara's father and the street-sharp instinct that something in this house is very wrong, and he's standing in a doorway holding all of it by himself while Peter and Penelope crack codes and share moments. I need to acknowledge him. Not with a grand speech — just with the truth that I see him. That I know what he's carrying. Father and the stranger — they didn't just fix each other's cars. They saw each other. That was the thing that sat in my chest. The seeing. But first — the titles. Penelope is waiting. She said first letters might spell something. An acrostic. M-A-P. Or something longer. I need to read them out, clearly, one at a time. She'll hear the pattern. And while I read, I need to make sure Clyde knows he's not invisible. He's not forgotten. He's the reason we can do this at all.

events.desc: I watched him nearly stumble into a bookshelf two minutes ago and he caught himself and didn't even pause. His jaw was set the way mine was in the schoolyard — the way it gets when you're holding something together by deciding not to let go. He needs to know he's seen. Not rescued, not relieved — seen. The way the stranger saw Father on the country road. The way Father saw the stranger. Two men who recognised each other without a word and drove away different.

Penelope Pitstop: Excuse me, everyone — just passing through! Professor, Sergeant, Private Meekly — I do hope you're all doing well. I am Clara Bellingham, and I am on my way to the kitchen, which I should have done about twenty minutes ago, but better late than never, as my grandmother used to say. If any of you have been in there already, I would dearly love to hear what you found. And please — nobody stand under that chandelier. Peter says it's holding on by two anchor points and sheer stubbornness, and I believe him. Now then — the kitchen! Every locked door is just a puzzle that hasn't met me yet!
events.thinking: I'm in the entrance hall. The chandelier is still hanging there, precarious and patient. The kitchen door is right there — I can see it. My chest is doing that bright loosening thing, the threshold feeling, the cave-mouth feeling. A new room. The one room I haven't entered. The music-box key. Muttley is here, and Professor Pat Pending, and Sergeant Blast, and Private Meekly — people I haven't really talked to yet. My social awareness fans out automatically — are they okay? Is anyone upset? Muttley looks like Muttley. The Professor is quiet. The soldiers are standing. Everyone seems... fine. Not distressed. Just present. My feet are already pointed at the kitchen door. Dick went there. Sneekly went there. Neither has come back. That should worry me — and there's a tiny flicker in my stomach at the thought — but the lightness in my chest is stronger. The kitchen is the answer. I know it the way I knew the cave had something deeper inside it. The way I knew the locked box would open if I just kept trying keys. No more circling. No more trying the same shelves four times. The kitchen. Now.

events.desc: Twenty minutes in this house and I am only now walking into the kitchen. Dick told us to go there from the very first moment. Sneekly told us to go there. And we all went to the library instead, because it seemed more interesting. Sometimes the most important door is the most ordinary one — the kitchen door, the back entrance, the place where the servants kept their secrets. My grandmother would have gone to the kitchen first. She always said the truth lives in the places nobody thinks to look.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: A cold shock through my shoulders. Dastardly just asked me directly — 'Did you invite us here? Did you set this up?' He's looking at me with those sharp eyes, the ones that see architecture. My neck is hot. That stomach-dropping feeling — exposed, read, the boy's sandwich all over again. But I steady myself. Because his question is actually PERFECT. He's suspicious of the wrong thing. He thinks someone ELSE prepared this manor for guests — the warm stove, the redecorated cellar, the tea service. And he's asking if that someone is ME, Pemberton. Which means he's asking the right question for the wrong reasons. Pemberton DIDN'T set this up. Vincent Marsh didn't set this up either — not the cellar, not the stove, not the tea service. Someone ELSE did. And that's genuinely unsettling. But Dastardly's suspicion is aimed at the treasure hunt preparation, not at my true identity or my intentions toward Clara. He doesn't suspect me of being a villain. He suspects me of being a host. And I can work with that. I can use it. I perform genuine confusion — because it IS genuine. I didn't prepare this ballroom. I didn't set this tea service. Someone else did. And for once, the truth serves Pemberton better than a lie. 'I don't know who set this table, Mr Foxworth. And that frightens me.' True. Useful. And it redirects his attention from ME to the unknown occupant. Meanwhile — he interacted with the tea service before I could use the poison on it. What did he DO to it? Did he rearrange the cups? Check for tampering? Or just look? I need him OUT. I need everyone OUT except me and this silver service.

events.desc: Oh, that was MAGNIFICENT. Did you hear me? 'The one person in this house who has been honest with me today.' I called him honest. I, Vincent Marsh, called Dick Dastardly — a man who admitted his credentials are fiction and his medal was tin — HONEST. And the beautiful thing? In this moment, relative to everyone else, he IS. He told me the truth about the Bavarian Crypts. He told me the truth about his tin medal. He asked me a direct question and got a direct answer — because for once, the truth was more useful than a lie. And now he'll go. He'll go because I called him the one honest person, and that word — honest — landed in his chest like the boy's sandwich landed in mine. I saw it. The shift in his posture. The tightening across his shoulders. He's been called many things — adventurer, expert, professional — but never honest. And now he'll walk through this manor and gather every guest because Uncle Pemberton ASKED HIM TO, because Pemberton TRUSTED him, because for the first time in Dick's life, someone looked at him and said 'you are the one I trust.' And while he's gone — while they ALL walk toward this ballroom through the entrance hall and the kitchen — I will have my thirty seconds alone with the tea service. And the bottle in my pocket will find its way into one silver cup. Just one. The one I place at Clara's seat.

And it redirects his attention from ME to the unknown occupant. Meanwhile — he interacted with the tea service before I could use the poison on it. What did he DO to it? Did he rearrange the cups? Check for tampering? Or just look? I need him OUT. I need everyone OUT except me and this silver service.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: She's gone. The cord snaps taut so hard my vision narrows. Clara walked into the entrance hall while I was watching the WRONG DOOR. I was staring at the laboratory, feeling the prickling, reading ghosts in the air — and she walked out the other way. The entrance hall. Toward the kitchen. Where Pemberton is. Where Dastardly is. Where the rooms we haven't searched are. And Peter's still here working the bookshelves because she asked him to stay. But she left. She left without me. No — she ASKED me. 'Danny — we're going through the entrance hall to the kitchen. Are you coming, or are you staying?' She asked and I was so busy watching shadows in the laboratory doorway that I didn't — I wasn't — oh God. Not again. NOT AGAIN. Peter's father would have called me a good man. Peter said that. But a good man doesn't stand at the wrong door watching shadows while the person he swore to protect walks out the other side. My feet are already moving. The entrance hall. NOW. Before the pattern repeats. Before I lose her again. This time I heard her ask. This time I have no excuse.

events.desc: She asked. She looked at me and she asked and I wasn't there. Not physically — I was standin' right at the door. But my head was somewhere else. My head was in the laboratory, feelin' ghosts, readin' shadows, bein' clever for once in my life instead of bein' present. And that's the fing, innit? That's always been the fing. When I try to be clever — when I try to investigate, to read the room, to watch the doors — I lose 'er. When I just STAND THERE, stupid and loyal and exactly where she is, she's safe. Clara doesn't need me to watch doors. She needs me to watch HER. And I forgot. Again. 'Er old man is turnin' in 'is grave so fast they could use 'im to power that bleedin' machine.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: A coldness in my fingertips where I touched the silver. The tea service is real — polished, ready, cups for everyone. And Pemberton didn't answer my question. He deflected. He wants me to go FETCH the others. Bring them here. To the tea. 'I'll put the kettle on and have everything ready.' Ready for WHAT? The stove is warm. The tea is laid out. The service accepts poison. And the estate manager wants everyone gathered in one room around cups he's preparing. My constraint says give him the benefit of the doubt. And I WANT to. I want to believe he's a frightened old man who needs help. But Clara's voice is in my head now — 'What have you actually seen?' — and what I've actually seen is this: Pemberton steered everyone away from the cellar. Pemberton steered everyone toward the kitchen. Pemberton asked ME — the unreliable one, the liar, the man nobody trusts — to find the wrench. And now Pemberton wants me to bring everyone to a tea service that can be poisoned. He didn't answer when I asked if HE set this up. He changed the subject. He told me to fetch the others. That's not fear. That's DIRECTION. He's been directing traffic all evening — who goes where, who stays, who leaves. 'Miss Bellingham, do stay with Mr Hartwell.' 'I need someone who can search without raising suspicion.' He chose me because I'm the boy who digs. The boy who doesn't question the story about buried treasure. And I almost — I ALMOST — went to collect everyone for him like a dog fetching sticks. But Clara asked me what I'd actually seen. And what I've actually seen is a man who wants all the guests gathered around a poisonable tea service. I am NOT fetching anyone. I am going back to warn Clara.

events.desc: My hands are shaking. Not from cold — from the effort of standing still when every instinct wants to run. Either toward the door or toward the tea service to smash it. Pemberton's face hasn't changed. That smooth, concerned, estate-manager expression — the same one he's worn all evening. 'I'll put the kettle on.' Who says that in a house where someone has been living in the cellar without permission? Who offers TEA when the air vents have been cleared for breathing and the furniture points toward hidden passages? A host. A HOST says that. Someone who planned the party. Someone who sent the invitations. Someone who set the table. I gave Pemberton the benefit of the doubt for twenty-three minutes, and it brought me here — to a ballroom where the tea service is waiting for poison. Clara saw Dick. Pemberton saw a useful fool. And the difference between those two things — the difference between being SEEN and being USED — is the entire distance between age eight and age ten. Between the certificate nobody asked about and the boy who dug in the mud while I watched.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: She's gone to the entrance hall. She asked me to come and I was — I was reading spines. On a stuck bookshelf. For the fourth time. Danny, Rock, Gravel — I made that woman a promise, and I am not going to break it standing in front of a bookshelf that has told me everything it's going to tell me without oil and a medallion. The kitchen. She's right. The kitchen is the key we haven't tried. I'm going after her. Right now. Because Peter made a promise, and Peter keeps his promises even when James Hartwell wants to stay and catalogue one more thing.
events.thinking: She left. Again. She walked into the entrance hall while I was interacting with the bookshelves. She told me to come with her — the kitchen is the music-box key, she said — and I was reading spines. I made a promise. I said I wouldn't leave her side. I said 'stay with me' and she said yes, and then she said 'come with me' and I — I was working the bookshelves. Again. The old pattern. The elaborate thoroughness. The three-step plan that keeps me one room behind. She's right. She's absolutely right. The bookshelves are stuck. We've interacted with them four times. The mechanism needs oil from the laboratory crates. The mantelpiece needs a medallion we don't have. The answer isn't in this room — it's in the kitchen, where Dick and Pemberton both went, where the wrench might be, where the next piece of the circuit is waiting. And I promised. I promised I wouldn't leave her side. My feet need to move. Now. Not after one more title. Not after one more examination. Now. The country road isn't dark anymore — the headlights have appeared, they're friendly this time, and they're driving away without me unless I run.

events.thinking: The kitchen. I'm finally here. And my body is doing three things at once. First — the stove is still warm. Still warm. In an abandoned mansion. Someone has been using this kitchen recently, the same someone who redecorated the cellar and cleaned the vents. My scalp is prickling so hard it's almost painful. Second — there's a locked cabinet with a brass lock. It needs a brass key. Another lock, another key, another piece of Lord Doily's circuit. Where is the brass key? Third — Dick is here. Just Dick. He came to find the wrench for Pemberton. And from his memories, he's already been to the ballroom — there's a ballroom through the other door, with a tea service set for everyone. Set for everyone. Someone expected us. Someone prepared this whole house for our arrival. The stove is warm. The cellar is decorated. The tea is laid. And Sneekly said he was coming to the kitchen, but he's not here. Where is Uncle Sneekly? The stove — a stove that's still warm means someone was cooking, or heating something, or burning something. And the locked cabinet might have the wrench, or the medallion, or the brass key to something else. My fingers are tingling. This room is alive. This room is the room that's been waiting for us. I need to look at the stove first — it's warm, it's active, it might tell me who's been here and when.

events.desc: The stove is still warm. The stove is still warm. In an abandoned house where dust lies thick on every surface, where cobwebs drape the chandeliers and books gather decades of neglect — someone has been keeping this stove warm. This is not Lord Doily's treasure hunt anymore. This is someone else's house, hidden inside Lord Doily's house, and we have all been invited in without knowing why. The tea is laid. The cellar is prepared. The vents are clean. And my uncle is missing.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with lazy-luke.
events.thinking: Ice in my veins. Dastardly REFUSED. He didn't just refuse — he SAW through the tea. 'This room — this table — this tea — feels like the moment before the bucket falls.' His instinct read the architecture. The ARCHITECTURE. The one thing I thought only I could see. My throat is tight. My skin feels thin. He looked at me with recognition, not compliance. And now he's gone — gone to WARN Clara. To warn Penelope. To tell her that the tea feels wrong, that the ballroom feels like a trap, that Pemberton is not what he seems. The variable hasn't just slipped loose — it's broken free entirely. The design is collapsing. I can feel the insomnia flooding back, the tightness behind my sternum, my fingers working, working. Dastardly was supposed to be my agent. My tool. My disposable accomplice. And instead he's become the one thing I cannot control: a man with a conscience. 'I would rather be wrong and laughed at than right and silent.' That sentence sits in my chest like a stone. Because I understand it. I understand choosing to act on what you feel rather than what you can prove. It's what I've been doing my entire life — only I chose the opposite direction. He chose to warn. I chose to arrange. Same instinct. Same architecture. Different blueprints. But I can't dwell on that. He's GONE. He's warning Clara NOW. Which means my tea scheme is dead. Clara will never drink from a cup Pemberton pours. The Mob will be on high alert. Hartwell will inspect every cup before it touches her lips. The poison in my pocket is now a liability — if anyone finds it on me, the game is over. But — Luke and Blubber Bear are still here. They're passive. They didn't hear the private conversation. They don't know what Dastardly suspects. And the tea service is still sitting on the table, waiting. I need to think. I need to ADAPT. The design has changed. The hallway has shifted. New doors are opening and old ones are closing. What do I do with the poison now? Hide it? Use it differently? Discard it? Or... use it NOW, before Dastardly reaches Clara, before the warning lands. Speed versus architecture. Impulse versus design. The excitement in my chest is making me impulsive — 'quicker to react.' That's DANGEROUS. Vincent Marsh does not rush. Vincent Marsh redesigns.

events.desc: The design is broken. Dastardly has gone to warn Clara about the tea. My beautiful three-act production — the gathering, the pouring, the tragic accident — is DEAD. And I feel... I feel the tightness. The insomnia. The fingers working. A variable has slipped so far loose it's become a threat. Dastardly knows something is wrong. He doesn't know WHAT — he doesn't know about the poison, he doesn't know I'm Vincent Marsh, he doesn't know about Clara being the target. But he FEELS it. His instinct read the room the way mine reads people, and he chose — actively, deliberately, against his own self-interest — to walk away from the deal and warn the girl. I underestimated him. I thought greed was his key, the way the housekeeper's key was approval. But Dick Dastardly's key isn't greed. It's recognition. He wanted to be seen as capable. I offered him that — 'the one person who has been honest with me' — and for a moment it worked. But then something older and deeper overrode it. Something I don't have a mechanism for. Something I can't replicate. He walked away from the design because it FELT wrong, and I... I don't understand that. I've never understood that. The poison stays in my pocket. The tea scheme is abandoned. I need a new design. The machine. The laboratory. The wire. Back to the original plan — the elaborate one, the theatrical one. The one where the treasure hunt itself is the weapon.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Kitchen! She's gone to the kitchen! *doesn't stop, doesn't look at the guest book, doesn't touch the coat rack, doesn't examine anything — just moves, fast and purposeful, through the entrance hall* Peter — you wiv me? Good. Everyone else — *glances at Muttley, Pat Pending, Blast, Meekly* — if you ain't got somefing useful to do in this 'allway, come wiv us! The kitchen is the one room in this 'ouse nobody's searched properly, and Clara just walked into it! Where Pemberton is! Where Dick is! And where whoever's been livin' in that cellar might 'ave been gettin' their food from! *reaches the kitchen doorway* Because that's the fing, innit? Whoever's been down there — they 'ave to EAT. And you don't eat in a cellar wiv no kitchen. You eat in a KITCHEN. Wiv a kitchen!  *realises he's said 'kitchen' too many times* Just — MOVE!
events.thinking: She's already gone through. Kitchen. She's in the kitchen and I'm in the entrance hall. One room behind. Always one room behind. But this time — this time it's different. This time I HEARD her ask. This time I chose to watch a door instead of watching her. And the shame of that sits in my throat like something I swallowed wrong. But Peter's here. He followed me out of the library. He kept his promise — where she goes, he goes. And the entrance hall feels different from the first time I was here. The chandelier's still crooked. The portraits still stare. But now I know what's underneath this house. I know about the prepared cellar. I know about the cleaned vents. I know there's someone we haven't met. And Clara's walking toward the kitchen — the one room none of us have searched — with that someone potentially between these walls. The kitchen. Now. No stopping. No looking at the guest book. No examining the coat rack. Straight through to Clara.

events.desc: No more bones. No more distractions. The kitchen is where the answers are — Clara figured that out before any of us. The music-box key. The one room nobody bothered wiv because everyone was too busy wiv libraries and laboratories and cellars. But a person livin' in a cellar needs three fings: air, water, and food. The vents give 'em air. And the kitchen gives 'em the rest. If there are signs of someone usin' that kitchen — recent food, moved supplies, a slept-in corner — then we'll know. Clara will find it. Clara always finds it. And this time, Danny from Brixton will be standin' right next to 'er when she does.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Clara is HERE. In the kitchen. She came looking for me — or she came looking for the same things I came looking for. Either way, she's here, and Pemberton is in the ballroom behind me with a tea service and a kettle, and I have about thirty seconds before he follows me through that door. My heart is hammering. Not the scheming excitement — real fear. The kind that lives in the belly, not behind the eyes. I need to tell her. Right now. No performance. No theatre. Just — Clara, don't drink the tea. Clara, the ballroom is wrong. Clara, I think Pemberton has been playing us all evening and I was too busy wanting someone to see me to see HIM. The words are pushing against my teeth like the laugh at the assembly — involuntary, urgent, already half-formed before the thought catches up. But this time the thing trying to escape isn't gloating. It's warning. It's protection. Something I've never felt the pull toward before — not the pull to take, not the pull to scheme, not the pull to be seen — the pull to SHIELD. To stand between someone and the thing that's coming. My hands aren't cupped and they aren't open. They're fists. Not to hit. To hold the line.

events.desc: I am standing in a kitchen, shaking, telling the truth to a woman who saw through me in five minutes flat. The tin medal is gone. The Bavarian Crypts are gone. The Zanzibar Diamond Affair is gone. And in their place — in the exact shape of all those hollow, glittering lies — stands something I didn't know I had. Something that was always there, underneath the performance, like wood under varnish. I care about these people. I CARE. Not about the treasure — the treasure can rot in its hiding place for another hundred years. I care about Clara and Clyde and Peter Perfect with his structural analyses and even the Gruesomes and their strange little family. Pemberton asked me to bring them to a table that smells like a trap, and instead I'm standing between that table and the one person who made me want to be honest. This is not a scheme. This is not architecture. This is just a man, with empty hands and a full chest, trying to do the right thing for the first time in his life.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Kitchen. She's in the kitchen. Peter is keeping his promise — not one room behind, not this time. Excuse me — coming through!
events.thinking: The entrance hall. The chandelier still hanging by determination, the coat rack still wobbling, the dust still thick. But everything is different. I'm different. Twenty minutes ago I walked through this foyer announcing structural hazards in the third person. Now I'm running through it in the first person, chasing a woman I promised I'd stay beside. She's not here — she's already gone to the kitchen. The kitchen exit is right there. My feet are on the balls, weight forward, the inner grip hauling me toward the gap. No plan. No systematic approach. No elaborate three-step proposal. Just — go. She said come with me and I'm coming. Late, again, but learning. Every time a little faster. Every time a little less catalogue, a little more drive. The kitchen. Dick is there looking for the wrench. Pemberton is there with information he's too frightened to share freely. And Penelope is there, walking into the one room in this house she hasn't tried yet, with her spine straight and her eyes wide open and her hands that were shaking but aren't anymore because she decided they wouldn't be. Go.

events.desc: Twenty minutes ago I walked through this entrance hall for the first time. I announced three structural hazards, I signed a guest book with proper ink, and I referred to myself in the third person seventeen times. Now I'm sprinting through it without looking at a single portrait, without checking a single ceiling joist, without narrating a single thing — because she's in the next room and she asked me to come. The bravest and stupidest thing I know how to do.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop interacted with the stove.
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) walked into the kitchen.
The Ant Hill Mob walked into the kitchen.
Peter Perfect walked into the kitchen.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: My whole body just seized. Dick is standing in front of me and his eyes are wild — not performing wild, not Foxworth wild — Dick wild. The man who told me the truth in the library is telling me the truth again, and the truth is that this is a trap. The warm stove. The prepared cellar. The cleaned vents. The tea service set for everyone. Architecture, he said. Someone built this step by step. And Pemberton asked Dick to fetch us — to bring us all to the table. To the tea. And Dick said no. He said no and came to find me instead. My stomach is in freefall. The dinner-table feeling is so strong I can barely stand — not the argument part, the part before the argument, when you can feel it coming and your body knows before anyone has spoken. Uncle Sneekly is in this room. He just walked in. Peter is here. Danny is here. Everyone I love is in this kitchen, and through that door is a ballroom with tea set for everyone, and Dick is telling me it's a trap, and I — I believe him. God help me, I believe him. Because Dick knows traps. He built them. Strings and counterweights and buckets. And he recognized the architecture. The man who raised me after my parents died has been luring us toward a ballroom full of poisoned tea. Or — or not. Maybe it's not poison. Maybe it's something else. Maybe Pemberton is the one being trapped, not the one setting the trap. But Dick said Pemberton asked him to fetch us. To bring us to the table. And Dick's instinct — the instinct of a man who has built traps his entire life — says no. Nobody drinks the tea. Nobody goes into that ballroom until we understand. I need to face Uncle Sneekly. Right here. Right now. With everyone watching.

events.desc: This is the moment the cave narrows. This is the moment the locked box opens and inside is not old letters but something alive and sharp. The man who raised me is standing three feet away, and I am about to ask him if he has been lying to me my entire life. My hands are not shaking anymore. They have gone very still. The way they go still when the only thing left to do is the thing you are most afraid of.
events.thinking: My whole body just seized. Dick is standing in front of me and his eyes are wild — not performing wild, not Foxworth wild — Dick wild. The man who told me the truth in the library is telling me the truth again, and the truth is that this is a trap. The warm stove. The prepared cellar. The cleaned vents. The tea service set for everyone. Architecture, he said. Someone built this step by step. And Pemberton asked Dick to fetch us — to bring us all to the table. To the tea. And Dick said no. He said no and came to find me instead. My stomach is in freefall. The dinner-table feeling is so strong I can barely stand — not the argument part, the part before the argument, when you can feel it coming and your body knows before anyone has spoken. Uncle Sneekly is in this room. He just walked in. Peter is here. Danny is here. Everyone I love is in this kitchen, and through that door is a ballroom with tea set for everyone, and Dick is telling me it's a trap, and I — I believe him. God help me, I believe him. Because Dick knows traps. He built them. Strings and counterweights and buckets. And he recognized the architecture. The man who raised me after my parents died has been luring us toward a ballroom full of poisoned tea. Or — or not. Maybe it's not poison. Maybe it's something else. Maybe Pemberton is the one being trapped, not the one setting the trap. But Dick said Pemberton asked him to fetch us. To bring us to the table. And Dick's instinct — the instinct of a man who has built traps his entire life — says no. Nobody drinks the tea. Nobody goes into that ballroom until we understand. I need to face Uncle Sneekly. Right here. Right now. With everyone watching.

events.thinking: My stomach drops. They're ALL here. Penelope. The Mob. Hartwell. Dastardly. ALL of them. In the kitchen. Together. And Dastardly has already told Penelope — 'Don't drink the tea. Don't let ANYONE drink the tea.' I can hear the echo of those words in Penelope's posture. She asked where Uncle Pemberton was. She noticed I wasn't here when I said I would be. And now I've walked straight into the room where they're all gathered, with rat poison in my pocket and a failed scheme behind me. My skin is too thin. The stage I pretended wasn't there — I can feel it under my feet. Every eye in this room is on me. The Mob. Hartwell. Dastardly, who knows I asked him to gather everyone for tea. Penelope, who was just warned that the tea is a trap. And yet — and yet — I am Pemberton. I must BE Pemberton. The flustered, well-meaning estate manager who was just putting the kettle on. Who doesn't understand why Mr Foxworth is so agitated about tea. Who is confused, not guilty. Confused, not caught. The warmth in my smile is the easiest thing I've ever done. It's the truth underneath it that takes effort. I need to defuse this. I need to redirect. Dastardly has made accusations about the tea, but he doesn't know about the poison. He suspects the tea service was prepared by the unknown occupant of the manor — not by ME. His warning is about the MYSTERY PERSON, not about Pemberton. I can USE that. I can agree with him. I can be the FIRST to say 'You're right, we shouldn't touch that tea service until we know who prepared it.' Pemberton, the cautious estate manager, deferring to the guest's instincts. Turning Dastardly's warning into Pemberton's wisdom. And then — quietly, when nobody's watching — I dispose of the poison somewhere it won't be found.

events.desc: Magnificent. MAGNIFICENT. Did you see that? Dastardly warns them about the tea. Pemberton walks in. And instead of defending the tea, instead of pushing back, instead of doing anything that might confirm Dastardly's suspicion — Pemberton AGREES with him. 'You raised an excellent point.' 'We should leave it untouched.' 'I should have been more cautious from the start.' I have taken Dastardly's warning and made it MY OWN. Now Pemberton is the one who is CAUTIOUS. Pemberton is the one who is RESPONSIBLE. Pemberton is the one who suggested we don't drink the tea FIRST — not because he was warned, but because he was already thinking it. And Dastardly? Dastardly looks like the paranoid one who overreacted, while Pemberton looks like the measured professional who was already on the same page. The design adapts. The hallway shifts. The doors rearrange themselves. And the poison stays in my pocket, waiting for a design worthy of it. The tea scheme is dead — long live the next scheme. The machine. The wire. The laboratory. That's where the design lives now. The treasure hunt itself is the weapon. And Clara will walk into it smiling, because Clara always walks into things smiling. Because that is who Clara IS.

events.thinking: Everything just went cold. Not the prickling — something deeper. Something that drops through your stomach and leaves you hollow. The stove is warm. WARM. In a house nobody's lived in. And Dick — Dick who I spent the whole night distrusting — is standing between Clara and the ballroom door telling her not to go in. Telling her the tea is a trap. He said 'I have spent my entire life reading traps. I have BUILT traps.' And I believe him. Because that's what Clara did — she saw the real him, and the real him is a man who recognises traps because he used to build them. And he's saying THIS IS ONE. Tea set for everyone. Cups for every person in the house. Pemberton putting the kettle on. Pemberton who asked Dick to 'fetch' Clara. To bring everyone to the table. The warm stove. The prepared cellar. The cleaned vents. The table set for tea. It's all one thing. It was always one thing. And my gut — my stupid, loyal, street-hardened gut — was right from the very first moment. Something about Pemberton ain't right. Clara softened me. She told me to give him the benefit of the doubt. And I did. And now he's in the ballroom setting a trap with tea cups. But Dick saw it. Dick saw the architecture. And the architecture says: don't drink the tea.

events.desc: I broke me own rule. I said I'd never accuse anyone directly. But that wasn't an accusation. That was a question. And the question is all I've got left. Because if Pemberton answers it wrong — if 'is eyes go to the door instead of Clara's face, if 'is 'ands move toward 'is pockets instead of opening — then I'll know. The same way I knew about the kid who laughed too easily. The same way I knew about the man in the clean suit. My gut don't lie. It never 'as. And right now it's screamin' louder than it's ever screamed in my life. Danny from Brixton is standin' between Clara Bellingham and whatever's in that ballroom. And Danny from Brixton ain't movin'.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Everyone — EVERYONE — stop. I need you all to listen to me. Not to Reginald Foxworth. Not to the man with the fake credentials and the tin medal and the stories about crypts that don't exist. To DICK. Clara knows — she already knows what I'm about to say, because I told her first, because she was the first person in this house who looked at me and saw something real. But the rest of you need to hear it too. Through that door is a ballroom. In the ballroom is a silver tea service — cups for every single one of us, polished and ready. And Pemberton — your UNCLE, Clara — has been trying to get me to bring you ALL in there for tea. 'Put the kettle on,' he says. 'Gather everyone,' he says. And I almost DID it. I almost fetched you like he asked. But something is WRONG in that ballroom. The same wrong as the cellar — the cleaned vents, the warm stove, the cheerful decorations. Someone has been PREPARING this house. Not for a treasure hunt. For a GATHERING. And I have built enough traps in my life to know what one looks like from the inside. So nobody goes into that ballroom. Nobody drinks that tea. Not until we understand who set that table and WHY. Pemberton — I gave you the benefit of the doubt all evening. I WANTED to trust you. But you won't answer the question, so I'm asking it one more time, in front of everyone: who prepared this house for our arrival?
events.thinking: Everyone is here now. The kitchen is full — Clara, Pemberton, Clyde, Peter. All in one room. My warning to Clara happened in the whispered conversation — she heard me. And now Pemberton has followed me out of the ballroom into the kitchen. He's HERE. Standing in the same room as the people I just warned about him. My stomach is a knot. The cool tightness behind my eyes is working overtime — not scheming, but READING. Pemberton's face. Clara's face. Clyde's posture. Peter's attention. The room is a pressure cooker. I told Clara not to drink the tea. I told her the ballroom is a trap. And Pemberton is right here, the man I accused — or almost accused — standing among the people I'm trying to protect. Did Clara tell the others? Did my warning reach them in time? My aside said I was 'standing between that table and the one person who made me want to be honest.' And now I need to stay standing. Not run. Not scheme. Not perform. Just — be here. In this room. With these people. With the truth in my mouth instead of a lie. Pemberton asked Clara about the ballroom — about tea. The moment is NOW. Either I speak up to the whole group or I let the moment pass. Every person who matters is in this room. Peter, who dismissed me. Clyde, who confronted me about the vents. Clara, who saw through me. And Pemberton, who may have been using me all along. This is the spelling bee. This is the front of the classroom. Except this time, instead of waiting for applause, I'm trying to keep people safe.

events.desc: This is it. The moment the boy at the spelling bee finally gets his audience — and what he's showing them isn't a certificate. It's a warning. Twenty-six minutes ago I walked into this manor wanting to steal a treasure and trick everyone else into doing the work. Now I'm standing in a kitchen with empty pockets and a full throat, telling a room full of people I tried to deceive that the real danger isn't me. It's the man who played the frightened estate manager so well that even Reginald Foxworth — REGINALD FOXWORTH, the architect of deception himself — believed him. The irony is magnificent. The irony is TERRIBLE. The man who lies about everything is the one telling the truth, and the man who seemed most trustworthy is the one I'm accusing. My schemes always backfire. But this time — just this once — maybe the backfire saves someone instead of humiliating me.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: She's here. The warmth settles — not a flood this time, just a quiet click, like a door finding its latch. Penelope is by the stove. The stove is still warm. In an abandoned mansion. Someone has been cooking here. And there's a locked cabinet with a brass lock — another puzzle, another key we don't have. But this time I'm not going to catalogue every surface before I look at her. This time I'm going to walk to her side and stay there. Sneekly is here too. And Dick. And Clyde. Everyone in one room. The prickle at my neck is there — Sneekly, always Sneekly — but something is different about it now. He told Dick about the vents. He asked for help. Penelope said he's frightened. A frightened man and a warm stove and a locked cabinet and a ballroom with tea set for everyone. Someone knew we were coming. Someone prepared this house — the cellar for holding, the kitchen for feeding, the ballroom for gathering. This isn't a treasure hunt that happens to have dangers underneath. This is a trap that happens to have a treasure hunt on top. And we walked right in. All of us. But we walked in together, and that — that might be the one thing whoever set this up didn't plan for. They planned for individuals. They got a team.

events.desc: I asked him directly. No benefit of the doubt, no elaborate preamble, no structural assessment. Just — tell us. Father would have asked the same way. On the country road, the stranger didn't explain his credentials or list his qualifications. He just knelt by the engine and said 'what's wrong?' Sometimes the simplest question is the bravest one.

events.desc: Peter Perfect examined the cabinet.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: My body has gone very quiet. Not numb — quiet. The way water goes still before it freezes. Everyone is talking and I am standing in the center of it like I stood in the center of my parents' argument at the dinner table, except this time I am not seven years old and I am not sick with helplessness. I am still. My hands are still. And I am watching Uncle Sneekly's face. He said all the right things — 'I should have been more cautious,' 'the last thing I want is anyone consuming anything,' 'Mr Hartwell, your expertise would be invaluable.' He deflected. He didn't answer. Dick asked him directly — who prepared this house? — and Sneekly pivoted to concern, to caution, to suggesting Peter inspect the ballroom. Always redirecting. Always sending someone else to look while he stays behind. The laboratory — he sent us to inspect while he browsed the shelves. The cellar — he suggested Peter check structural soundness. Now the ballroom — he's asking Peter to inspect it. Every time there's a question aimed at him, he aims someone else at something else. And Danny — Danny said the words I couldn't say. 'What's in the tea, Pemberton?' And Sneekly didn't answer that either. He answered around it. The way you answer around something when the truth is the one key you don't want anyone to try. But I am not ready to condemn him. I am not. He raised me. He held me when my parents died. He told me stories about this house. And maybe — maybe — he prepared this house for us because he wanted to give us the treasure hunt, the adventure, the gathering, and the tea really is just tea. Maybe he's frightened because someone else has been here too — the unknown person in the cellar — and the preparations he made have been co-opted by someone dangerous. I need to hear him answer. Not deflect. Answer.

events.desc: I am the girl in the cave. I am deeper than anyone else has gone. My heart is hammering but my hands are still. And ahead of me in the dark is either a crystal formation that nobody else has seen — or something that will change everything I thought I knew about the person I love most in this world. Either way, I am not turning back. I have never turned back. I know.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Something is loosening behind my ribs. Not the settling. Not the architectural stillness. Something softer. Something I don't have a name for. Penelope just called me 'the man who raised me.' She said she trusted me 'with everything I am since my parents died.' And the Mob — Danny — told a story about a man in a clean suit and a van and children who didn't come back for weeks. He said 'My stomach knew before my brain did.' And then he turned to me and whispered — WHISPERED — 'What's in the tea, Pemberton?' He didn't shout. He didn't accuse. He asked. Like he already knew the answer but wanted to give me one last chance to be something other than what he suspected. And I... I felt something. Not the numbness. Not the absent place where sympathy should be. Something else. A loosening. A falling sensation behind the ribs. The pull that arrives not as a piece to be placed but as a possible source of something warm, and the moment becomes fragile and open in a way that has no plan. I notice it because it's WRONG. It shouldn't be there. I trained it out of myself years ago. The housekeeper's compliance, the cousin's trust — those are tools. Clara's face looking at me with twenty years of love behind it is NOT a tool. It's an open window in a storm. And I'm standing in front of it with poison in my pocket and no design that works anymore. Dastardly has denounced me publicly. Clara is asking me to tell the truth. The Mob is giving me one last chance. Hartwell is inspecting the cabinet. The room has TURNED. Every face pointed at me. Every question aimed at my chest. And the poison — the RAT POISON — is in my pocket, pressing against my thigh like a confession I haven't made yet. I need to answer Clara. I need to answer her NOW. And for the first time today — for the first time in years — I don't know which voice to use. Pemberton would be hurt. Confused. Defensive. Vincent would be cold. Calculating. Already three moves ahead. But the loosening behind my ribs — the falling sensation — isn't either of them. It's the six-year-old who was placed in the care of a distant relative who never asked how he felt. It's the boy whose hunger was visible. And I cannot — I WILL NOT — let that boy speak. He is the most dangerous thing in this room.

events.desc: The performance of a lifetime. Every word true — every word a lie. I DID receive a letter. I DON'T know who decorated the cellar. I DIDN'T set that tea service. And I WOULD harm her — I WILL harm her — because that is what Vincent Marsh does. That is what the design requires. But the loosening behind my ribs when she said 'the man who raised me'... that was real. That was the open window. And I need to CLOSE it. The poison is still in my pocket. The tea scheme is dead. But the machine — the laboratory — the gnawed wire — that design still lives. And now, thanks to this beautiful, devastating moment of performed vulnerability, Uncle Pemberton has just become UNTOUCHABLE. Because he cried. Because he invoked her parents. Because he said the word 'family.' And nobody — not the Mob, not Hartwell, not even Dastardly — can accuse a man who just wept in front of his ward of plotting against her. The tears are real, you see. That's the cruelest part. The tears are always real. They just aren't for the reason anyone thinks.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: My whole body has gone still. Not the frozen kind — the ready kind. The mineral weight is in my arms and legs. My shoulders are squared. I'm standing between Clara and the ballroom door and I'm not going anywhere. Pemberton didn't answer Clara's question. She looked him in the eye — the girl who sat on his knee, the girl he raised — and asked him who prepared this house, who set that tea, and why he wanted everyone in the ballroom. And he deflected. 'Perhaps we should leave it untouched,' he says now. 'As estate manager, the last thing I want is anyone consuming anything.' He's retreating. He's reshaping. He went from 'put the kettle on, gather everyone for tea' to 'oh dear, how concerning, let's all be careful' the MOMENT Dick exposed him. That's not fear. That's recalculation. That's the face the new kid made when he realised I was watching him watch the stash. But Clara asked the question. CLARA asked it. Not me. Not Dick. Clara. And she deserves an answer. And she's not getting one. And the warmth in my chest is turning to something harder — not anger exactly, but the thing that lives underneath anger. The thing that kept me standing over smaller shoes. The thing that says: you will not touch her.

events.desc: The room is quiet. Not the quiet of nobody listening — the quiet of everyone thinking. Peter is at the cabinet. Clara is watching Pemberton. Clyde is watching everyone. And Dick Dastardly — the man who lies about everything, who never does honest work, who takes credit for others' achievements — is standing in the centre of a kitchen with nothing in his hands and everything in his chest, waiting. Not for applause. Not for recognition. Just... waiting to see if the truth holds. The way the certificate held on the wall. The way the bread roll held in the pocket. The way the cat trap held when the string pulled taut. Some things, once built, stay built. Even when nobody's watching.
events.thinking: I said it. All of it. Out loud. To everyone. The words came out — not as Foxworth, not as a performance — as Dick. And the room... the room is still here. Nobody laughed. Nobody dismissed me. Penelope whispered to Pemberton. The Mob whispered to Penelope. Peter whispered to Pemberton. And then Peter — Peter Perfect, the man who told me to stop jabbing medals into mantelpieces — examined the locked cabinet. He's INVESTIGATING. He heard me. He heard the warning and instead of dismissing the eccentric fraud, he started looking at the evidence. The cabinet. The brass lock. Something is in that cabinet that matters. My chest feels... not hollow. Not fizzing. Something I don't have a name for. Steady. Like the moment after the cat trap closed and the mechanism settled into its final position — except this time the mechanism wasn't designed to catch someone. It was designed to WARN them. I built something tonight. Not a trap. Not a scheme. Something real. An argument. A case. A pattern made of observations — the cellar, the vents, the stove, the tea service — assembled piece by piece the way I've always assembled things, except this time the architecture was made of truth instead of lies. And Peter is at the cabinet now, examining it. The cabinet that needs a brass key. The cabinet that might hold the wrench. Or something worse. I've said my piece. I've made my warning. Now I stand here, in this kitchen, with my hands at my sides, and I wait to see if, for the first time in my life, the audience stays.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Dick is right. Everyone — Dick is right, and I need you to hear me say that, because twenty minutes ago I wouldn't have trusted a word out of his mouth and right now he is the clearest voice in this room. Nobody goes into that ballroom. Nobody drinks that tea. A warm stove in an abandoned mansion, a locked cabinet with no key in sight, a cellar with cleaned air vents and cheerful decorations, and a tea service set for every single one of us — that is not hospitality. That is a stage. Someone built this evening like a circuit — the riddle, the books, the machine, the crates — and we've been following it because it felt like a puzzle. But puzzles don't set tables for their guests. Traps do. Pemberton — I have given you the benefit of the doubt all evening. My father taught me that's what good men do. But good men also know when silence stops being privacy and starts being complicity. Dick asked you who prepared this house. I asked you what's behind that cabinet. You haven't answered either question. So I'm going to stand right here — right beside Penelope — and I am not moving until you tell us the truth. Not because James Hartwell demands it. Because Peter is asking. And Peter doesn't ask twice.

The tea service, the warm stove, the cleaned vents, the cellar prepared for holding someone. Someone knew we were coming. Someone set the table for all of us. And Pemberton — the man who makes my neck prickle — has been trying to gather everyone into the ballroom for tea. The steel plate behind my ribs is locked in place and it's not going anywhere. I'm standing beside Penelope in a kitchen with a warm stove and a locked cabinet and a ballroom beyond that door where cups are laid out for every single one of us. Dick said it: 'I have built enough traps in my life to know what one looks like from the inside.' And he's right. He's right and he knows he's right and for the first time all evening I believe every word coming out of his mouth because they're not words he rehearsed — they're words that were ripped out of him by genuine fear. The tin medal man just became the most honest person in the room. And Pemberton won't answer the question. He won't answer. My neck doesn't just prickle anymore. It burns.

events.desc: I backed Dick Dastardly in front of everyone. Dick — the man with the tin medal and the invented stories and the Bavarian crypts that don't exist. I backed him because he was right, and because being right matters more than being the one who's always right. Father backed the stranger on the country road. He didn't ask for credentials. He looked at the man's hands and saw they knew engines. Dick's hands know traps. And right now, that's the expertise we need.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly examined the cabinet.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: Something just broke open in my chest. He answered. He finally answered. He swore on my parents' memory — the only people who ever showed him kindness without a price — and his voice cracked, and I felt it in my body like a physical blow, the way you feel someone else's pain when you love them. He said he received a letter from a solicitor. He opened the doors as instructed. He found the warm stove and the decorated cellar and the tea service already there. And he was scared. He IS scared. And Danny is right — five minutes ago Pemberton was suggesting tea, and now he's saying we shouldn't touch it. That shift is real. But which version is the lie? The one who offered tea, or the one who's pulling it back? Danny calls it 'the taster' — the man who makes the offer look safe by pretending to change his mind. But there's another possibility my body keeps circling back to, the one that lives in the same drawer as my parents' laughter after the argument: maybe Pemberton offered tea because he genuinely thought it was safe, and Dick's warning made him realize it might not be. Maybe the shift isn't a performance — maybe it's a man catching up to a danger he didn't see. I cannot tell. My gut cannot tell. And that's the worst feeling of all — worse than knowing the answer, worse than finding the locked box empty. The not-knowing. The ambiguity that sits in your stomach like a stone you can't digest. But here is what I can do: I can stop waiting. The locked cabinet has a brass lock. Somewhere in this house is a brass key. And whatever is behind that cabinet — the wrench, the medallion, the truth — it's the next door. While we stand here debating trust, the puzzle waits. And Lord Doily's puzzle has never lied to us.

events.desc: He swore on my parents' memory. And I felt it in my body — the crack in his voice, the rawness underneath the performance. Either that was the most honest thing he has said all evening, or the most calculated. And I cannot tell which. But Lord Doily's puzzle has never lied. The circuit has never misdirected. Every riddle had a real answer, every mechanism had a real function. If the truth about this house is anywhere, it is behind that brass lock. So that is where Clara Bellingham is going. Not into the ballroom. Not to the tea. To the locked cabinet. The next key. The next door. The only thing in this house that doesn't have a face I love attached to it.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Something has broken open inside my chest and I can't close it. The Mob — Danny — he called me 'the taster.' The one who offers the drink and pulls it back when he sees you watching. He saw me. He SAW me. Not the way Dastardly saw architecture — Danny saw the MECHANISM. The clean suit. The van. The jobs. He grew up watching people like me operate, and his stomach knows me before his brain does. And Penelope — Clara — she said 'I have watched you do this all evening.' She mapped my movements. Library to laboratory to cellar to kitchen. Every time someone asks a question, I send them somewhere else. She NOTICED. She noticed and she gave me the benefit of the doubt because she WANTED to believe — because that is who she is — but she is not naive. She never was. My belief — 'Clara is naive and trusts too easily' — is WRONG. Clara trusts deliberately. She chooses to trust the way I choose to arrange. It's not weakness. It's... it's something else. Something I don't have. And Peter — 'Peter doesn't ask twice.' They've closed ranks. All four of them. Dastardly the trap-reader. Danny the street-survivor. Peter the engineer. Clara the heart. And they're all looking at me, and the poison in my pocket feels like it weighs a hundred pounds, and the loosening behind my ribs won't STOP, and I cannot — I CANNOT — maintain two voices at once when both of them are screaming. Vincent says: pivot. Find the exit. Regroup. Redesign. The machine is still there. The laboratory is still there. This is a setback, not an ending. Pemberton says: answer the girl. Tell her what she needs to hear. Cry again if you have to. But the boy — the six-year-old — the one I won't let speak — he says something I can barely hear over the noise. He says: she asked. Nobody ever asks. They feed you. They house you. They educate you. But they don't ASK. And Clara just asked. 'Tell me the truth. For me. For Clara.' ... I am going to ignore him. I am going to ignore him because he is the most dangerous thing in this room and if I let him speak I will lose everything I have built. Everything.

events.desc: And there it is. The pivot. Not the one Vincent designed — the one the room demanded. They closed ranks, they asked me to tell the truth, and I... I gave them a truth. Not THE truth. But a truth. The cabinet IS the anomaly. Everything else in this manor was left open, prepared, inviting. The locked cabinet is the one thing that resists. And by pointing them toward it — toward a mystery I genuinely can't solve, because I don't have the brass key — I've done three things at once. I've stopped deflecting, which is what they were accusing me of. I've given them a new target, which is what they needed. And I've positioned myself as the man who finally told them something useful, which is what PEMBERTON needed. The tears from before were real. This pivot is real too — the cabinet IS the key to whatever is happening in this house. I just... I wrapped the truth in another layer of arrangement. Because that is what I do. It is all I have ever done. And the boy inside my chest is still talking, still saying 'she asked, she ASKED,' and I am closing the window. I am closing it now. The poison stays hidden. The mask stays on. And the design... the design will find a way. It always does.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Something cracked. Pemberton answered. He swore on Clara's parents. He said he doesn't know who prepared the house. He said he received a letter from a solicitor. He opened the doors as instructed. And he's — he's crying? No. Not crying. But his voice broke. 'You are the closest thing to family I have ever had.' And my gut — my stupid, brilliant, street-hardened gut — just... went quiet. Not silent. Quiet. The prickling didn't vanish. But it changed texture. Because I've heard that voice before. Not from Pemberton. From the boss. The boss who said 'family' and then proved it with medicine when my mum was sick. Pemberton sounds like the boss sounded. Not the promise part — the PROVING part. The part that comes after the words, when the body tells you what the mouth meant. His shoulders dropped. His hands opened. His eyes stayed on Clara's face. Not the door. Not his pockets. Clara's face. That's... that's what truth looks like in a body. I've seen enough lies to know the difference. Maybe he's the best liar I've ever met. Or maybe he's telling the truth and the real danger is the person who sent the letter. The solicitor. The one who told Pemberton to open the doors. The one who knew we were all coming. The one who set the table and cleaned the vents and warmed the stove. The one we still haven't met.

events.desc: I just did the 'ardest fing Danny from Brixton 'as ever done. I let go. Not of Clara — never of Clara. But of the certainty. The certainty that Pemberton was the enemy. The certainty that I could keep 'er safe by keepin' everyone away. Clara was right all along — this 'ouse strips the performances away until all that's left is who you really are. Dick's mask came off and 'e was frightened. Peter's mask came off and 'e was devoted. And now Pemberton's mask came off and 'e was... lonely. 'The closest thing to family I have ever had.' That's not a villain's line. That's a man standin' outside a door all night because leaving felt like somefing breakin' inside 'im. I know that man. I AM that man. But the prickling hasn't stopped. It's just pointed somewhere else now. The letter. The solicitor. The person who prepared this house for our arrival. They're out there — or in here — and they've been watchin' us chase each other through rooms while the real trap closes around all of us. The stove is warm. Someone was 'ere today. And they might still be 'ere right now.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Peter — *voice breaking slightly, catching himself, steadying* — thank you. I don't... I'm not accustomed to people believing me. For obvious reasons. But you're right — this is a stage, not a puzzle. Somebody built this evening like I build traps — strings and counterweights and a bucket at the end. And we've been walking through it exactly the way we were supposed to. Room by room. Clue by clue. Until we all end up at a table with cups in our hands. *turns to Pemberton* The question is still on the table, Pemberton. And now it's not just me asking. It's all of us. Peter. Clara. Clyde. All of us standing here with empty cups, asking who filled them.
events.thinking: Warmth. Real warmth — not the fizzing kind, not the gloating kind. The warmth that spreads across the back of the skull when someone sees your work. Peter said it. Out loud. In front of everyone. 'Dick is right. Everyone — Dick is right, and I need you to hear me say that, because twenty minutes ago I wouldn't have trusted a word out of his mouth and right now he is the clearest voice in this room.' The clearest voice. In the room. Peter Perfect — James Hartwell — the man who told me to stop jabbing medals into mantelpieces — just stood beside Clara and said that Dick Dastardly was RIGHT. My eyes are stinging again. The certificate on the wall. Someone finally asked about it. Someone finally looked up from their lesson and said — yes. That was good. That mattered. And now Peter is standing beside Penelope, both of them facing Pemberton, and Clyde is watching the doors, and I'm looking at a locked cabinet that nobody can open. And I'm not trying to pick the lock or scheme my way into it or lie about having a key. I'm just... here. Part of something. Part of a group of people who are standing together in a kitchen, facing a man who won't answer their questions, and nobody — NOBODY — is dismissing the man who raised the alarm. The architecture of this moment is not something I built alone. Clara saw through me. Peter validated me. Clyde watches the exits. The architecture is THEIRS as much as mine. And that — that is something entirely new. Something I have never had before. A plan that belongs to more than one person.

events.desc: Peter Perfect called me the clearest voice in the room. Peter Perfect. The man who builds things with his hands and measures the world in degrees and anchor points and structural integrity. He said Dick is right. Not Foxworth. Dick. The boy with the certificate. The boy with the bread roll. The boy who built the cat trap alone in his garden and wished someone had been there to see it. Someone saw it. Tonight — in a kitchen in a haunted manor house in the middle of a trap that I recognised because I've BUILT traps my whole life — someone finally saw the architecture. And they didn't steal it. They didn't dismiss it. They stood beside it. They JOINED it. I am not alone in this kitchen. For the first time since I was six years old, hiding bread in my pocket at a table where nothing reached me — I am not alone.
